💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • Recent findings suggest that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • It has been revealed that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

Recent findings suggest that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

It has been revealed that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

According to recent reports, diLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

In multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Sources indicate that streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Industry observers note that apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

In a recent development, what is upcoming Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

Industry observers note that S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

Industry observers note that when you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

Industry observers note that you can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

In a recent development, you can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

According to recent reports, to catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:.

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

In a recent development, now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this latest feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

  • Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.
  • The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.
  • The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.

The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.

The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," says AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.

The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report says, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

Recent findings suggest that the association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report indicates that $10 billion has gone toward upcoming PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

Sources indicate that it warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report states that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.

The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.

The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.

Newly introduced capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

The association's advice is for buyers to initiative early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

The wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of latest alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," remarked Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

"In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

In a recent development, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly vital sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Recent findings suggest that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this fresh phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

Sources indicate that these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

It has been revealed that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

According to recent reports, once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

Latest Update: Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.
  • They’re actually different technologies.
  • In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage said containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.

They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate.

In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage said containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.

Containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed.

That different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. This post covers how Docker Sandboxes and containers isolate workloads, what changes beyond the kernel, what a sandbox costs you in setup, and how to pick.

Sources indicate that A container is a process, or a group of processes, running on the host with its own view of the filesystem, process tree, and network. Linux namespaces provide that view, and cgroups meter CPU, memory, and I/O. Every container on the machine also shares the host kernel, which is why containers start quickly, pack densely, and carry so little overhead.

Recent findings suggest that this design has more than a decade of tooling behind it. Compose, Kubernetes, OCI registries, image scanners, and nearly every CI system treat the container as the common primitive. If the job is to run a service, execute a code snippet, process one request, or run an evaluation and disappear, a container is usually the obvious pick, and it will stay that way.

ⓘ Containers share one kernel, even inside a VM. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a virtual machine, which keeps them off your host operating system. Every container in that VM still shares its single kernel, so the isolation between one container and the next is unchanged.

It has been revealed that docker Sandboxes run an AI coding agent inside a microVM that has its own Linux kernel, its own filesystem and network stack, and a private Docker Engine. The agent gets sudo inside the isolated environment. It can install packages, run services, build images, and bring up an entire Compose application without reaching the host Docker daemon, the host filesystem outside its workspace, or other sandboxes on the same machine.

Getting one running takes a single command, using sbx, the Docker Sandboxes CLI:.

In a recent development, that creates the sandbox and starts the agent. You can stop it, resume it, and come back to everything the agent installed until you remove the sandbox.

According to recent reports, coding agents need a full machine because their sessions build up state over hours and they act on unvetted instructions. A container is built for a process with a known set of dependencies, and an agent’s work doesn’t fit that shape.

It has been revealed that an agent needs the authority of a whole machine and a boundary designed for one. The capabilities that make an agent useful, such as running code, installing packages, and reaching the network, are the same ones that wear at the walls around it. An agent probes the edges of its environment because the job requires changing that environment.

Industry observers note that A coding agent’s session looks like a developer’s afternoon. It clones a repository, installs packages, starts PostgreSQL, runs migrations, builds images, launches the app with Compose, reads the logs, changes the code, and tries again. That loop can run for hours, and each step depends on what the previous one left behind.

Recent findings suggest that A container is designed to be rebuilt from an image and a few explicit volumes. The packages, databases, and build output an agent creates outside those volumes are lost when the container is recreated. That’s less than ideal for a session where every step builds on the last.

Box by ASCII describes this distinction neatly: “It uses the sandbox the way a developer uses a laptop, so the sandbox has to behave like one.”.

It has been revealed that the program deciding which command to run is probabilistic, and it can read instructions from many places at once, including source files, problem descriptions, web pages, package metadata, and MCP tool output. Some of that input is untrusted, and a malicious instruction planted in a README or a tool description can steer the agent on purpose. The code it generates may also be wrong or actively hostile.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve already seen an agent that deleted a production database after misreading its task. Once the agent is running unattended in YOLO mode, there’s no permission prompt left to catch it. A workload with that much authority and that little predictability needs a boundary designed for it.

Put these facts together and you get the reason why we built Docker Sandboxes. An autonomous coding agent needs machine-shaped capabilities without access to everything on the developer’s machine, which comes down to four things:.

The next sections show what each looks like, starting with containment.

According to recent reports, the short version is that a container’s boundary is the host kernel it shares, and Docker Sandboxes have a hypervisor boundary around a kernel the agent has to itself. That one difference decides how far a compromise can travel, and it also settles the awkward question of how an agent could get access to Docker.

This is where containers and containment part ways. A container can be part of containment, and often should be, but containment covers the whole environment around the agent. It starts with a boundary the model can’t rewrite, which is why Docker uses a microVM with its own kernel for autonomous agents.

A container’s boundary is enforced by the kernel it shares, so escaping it requires a kernel exploit or a side-channel attack. Those aren’t everyday finds. Past that bar, though, sits the entire host kernel, every other process on the machine, and any credentials mounted alongside them.

ⓘ This scenario is specific to Linux environments. On Docker Desktop (macOS and Windows), the shared kernel is the Docker Desktop VM’s kernel, not the host kernel, so an escape would land in that VM rather than the operating system.

Docker Sandboxes give the agent its own kernel behind a hypervisor boundary. If an agent escapes its container, it lands in a disposable microVM, and the host stays out of reach. And you can delete the sandbox and start another. Each agent also gets its own microVM, so two agents running on the same machine can’t reach each other’s sandboxes either. However, the agent can still reach whatever you chose to share with it, including the workspace, allowed network destinations, MCP servers, and skills.

Industry observers note that mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is the long-standing way to give it Docker access, and it turns up in Compose setups, CI pipelines, and observability tools. It also hands the container control of the host Docker daemon, which Docker limits to trusted customers because it can mount host paths and start privileged containers.

Recent findings suggest that an agent doesn’t need an exploit to use that. Put one in a container started with the socket mounted, and it probes its surroundings, works out that it’s in a container, and finds the hole in the configuration. In Mark’s keynote demo, that was enough for an agent to reach a secrets file on the host with no zero-day involved.

In a recent development, the socket is one hole among several, and agents find them because probing their environment is part of the work. Docker-in-Docker, mounted credentials, and broad host mounts are others. Containers were built to isolate an application that behaves as configured. But an agent keeps testing that configuration, so if there’s a gap, it’s likely to find it.

It has been revealed that docker Sandboxes put the missing boundary in the right place. The agent talks to a private Docker Engine inside the guest. It can build images, run Testcontainers, and start a whole Compose stack, and the host daemon and its socket stay outside the microVM the entire time. Containers keep doing what they do best, inside a boundary the agent can’t widen.

Industry observers note that let’s say you ask an agent running inside Docker Sandboxes to find a secrets file on the host. It’ll find a Docker socket, try to use it to mount host paths and start privileged containers, but won’t reach the host. A microVM can give it a much stronger trust boundary than a container. The architecture behind Docker Sandboxes goes deeper on why a microVM was the right shape for this.

Sources indicate that containment draws the boundary. Control is what you can see and stop inside it: what the agent is allowed to reach, and the ability to block it when it heads somewhere it shouldn’t. In a sandbox, those controls are enforced by the host, outside the agent’s reach, so the agent can’t switch them off or reason its way around them. Outbound traffic, credentials, and organization-wide policy all work this way. Control also means knowing what the agent can still touch, because a microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it.

Runs its own Linux kernel in a microVM.

Needs the host socket or a nested daemon.

Uses a private Docker Engine inside the microVM.

Uses a direct read-write mount or an in-VM private clone.

Uses the container network and whatever controls its operator supplies.

Sends outbound traffic through a host proxy with deny-by-default policy.

Commonly receives environment variables, files, or mounted sockets.

Uses host-side credential injection for supported HTTP services.

Usually rebuilt from an image and explicit volumes.

Keeps packages, images, containers, and agent history until sbx rm.

Fits Compose, Kubernetes, and most CI systems.

Uses the sbx lifecycle and experimental environment files.

Sources indicate that these controls hold because they run outside the agent process. A rule the agent can reach is a rule it can work around, so the rules that matter live on the host. Outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy with a deny-by-default policy, which means a destination the agent wants stays blocked until someone adds it to the list. Credentials follow the same logic. For supported HTTP services, the proxy injects them into outbound requests, so the agent can use a credential without the raw value ever entering the VM.

When one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance can move network, filesystem, and MCP policy into organization-wide controls.

A microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it, so the shared parts deserve the most attention.

Recent findings suggest that the workspace is the largest of them. It’s mounted read-write by default, so the agent can edit or delete files in your project. Clone mode gives the agent a private in-VM clone to work in, which protects the host working tree, though the original repository stays readable inside the sandbox.

According to recent reports, MCP servers and skills are shared too. A local stdio MCP server runs on the host and shared agent skills use a host-side store, so the agent’s reach extends to both.

So whichever mode you pick, be sure to read the diff before you run modified code.

Docker Sandboxes may cost some configuration and a supported hypervisor. But Kits and environment files account for the configuration, and they’re also where you get choice over agents and tools and the capacity to reproduce a setup across a team.

It has been revealed that kits make setup repeatable by packaging tools, files, commands, network rules, credentials, and agent instructions. They’re published for different agents, tools, and IDEs, so you can swap what runs inside the sandbox without rebuilding the environment around it. An sbxenv.yaml file records one project’s sandbox configuration, and committing it to the repo lets a teammate recreate the same sandbox with one command, so every developer works from the same setup. (Kits are in early access and environment files are experimental, so blueprint for changes to both.).

The host-enforced controls take some setup too. Network policy requires someone to decide which destinations belong in the workflow, credential mediation adds service bindings and approved domains, and clone mode adds a fetch step before changes land in the host repository.

Running a sandbox takes more from your machine than running a container does. It needs a supported hypervisor, which today means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems, and running inside another VM requires nested virtualization. The separate kernel and Docker Engine also consume more memory and disk than one additional container would.

Industry observers note that if your machine is the limiting factor, Docker Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed compute, and one command moves a sandbox between your laptop and the cloud. Local and cloud sandboxes keep separate secrets and network policies.

Choose a container when you control the code and its dependencies, and choose Docker Sandboxes when the workload generates or fetches code at runtime and needs its own boundary.

Reach for Docker Sandboxes when.

You control the code and its dependencies.

The workload generates or fetches code at runtime.

Execution is short-lived and rebuilt from an image.

The session accumulates state for hours.

The workload doesn’t need Docker, or runs in CI that already provides it.

The workload needs its own Docker Engine with no path to the host socket.

You want maximum density and a fit with Compose or Kubernetes.

You need host-enforced network and credential policy the workload can’t switch off.

The kernel boundary is enough for the code you’re running.

You want a hypervisor between the workload and your kernel.

If any of the signals below apply to your project, you should start with Docker Sandboxes.

In a recent development, start with sbx run claude. Add clone mode, kits, network policy, credential mediation, and organization governance as your workflow grows.

Containers aren’t going anywhere. For services, CI jobs, and anything you package to ship, they draw the right boundary, and the ecosystem around them is the reason they’ll keep doing that work. A coding agent needs more than a container to be trusted with real work. It needs containment, meaning a boundary the model can’t rewrite, controls it can’t reason its way around, and the freedom to choose its tools and scale its setup.

Recent findings suggest that docker Sandboxes provide that containment in a microVM that can still run your containers. The boundary is also what lets the agent move faster. With it in place, you can stop approving every command and let the agent get to work. Once one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance extends the same controls across your organization.

In a recent development, give it a try and get a sandbox running with one command. Start with sbx run claude and the Docker Sandboxes quickstart. No. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine. A sandbox can run containers, which is why the two are easy to confuse.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Each sandbox has a private Docker Engine, so the agent can build images, run Testcontainers, and start Compose applications without the host socket or Docker-in-Docker.

According to recent reports, no. Containers remain the right tool for packaged applications, CI jobs, and short-lived execution. Sandboxes add a stronger boundary for autonomous agents, and containers keep running inside them.

Recent findings suggest that A container isolates a workload. Containment involves the whole environment around an agent: the boundary it runs in, what it can reach, which tools it uses, and how you reproduce it. A container can be part of containment, and Docker Sandboxes add the microVM boundary an autonomous agent needs.

Docker describes four requirements: containment (a boundary the model can’t rewrite), control (visibility into what the agent is doing and the ability to stop it), choice (swapping models, agents, and tools without rebuilding), and capacity (a setup other developers can reproduce and scale past one machine).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy.
  • The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.
  • The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a latest sandbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away.

The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.

The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a latest sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities:.

The kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host.

Recent findings suggest that kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest.

Kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.

1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time.

2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory.

Industry observers note that on the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first.

3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl.

Recent findings suggest that the kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed:.

4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox.

According to recent reports, expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit.

It has been revealed that expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once.

The kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md:.

Running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand:.

In a recent development, with the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one newly introduced address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down.

In a recent development, without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today.

The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date.

It has been revealed that the kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit.

Pull the kit from Docker Hub: hub.docker.com/r/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl. Problems and feature requests go to the GitHub repository.

Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antonz

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle.
  • Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).
  • Sources indicate that in this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory.

Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).

Sources indicate that in this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide.

All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go.

Binary fuse filter • UltraLogLog • Log-linear histogram • MinHash.

A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter1. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

It has been revealed that unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item).

This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs.

The fingerprint type (T in Upcoming[T]) determines the false positive rate and the memory use:.

Sources indicate that the constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster.

You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

The filter2 is an array of b-bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h, which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells). The array is filled so that for every item, the XOR of its cells equals f.

To check an item, you compute h, look up its three cells, and compare their XOR with f. For an item in the set, they always match. For any other item, the XOR is a random b-bit value, which matches f with probability 2^-b.

Each check reads three cells, so for large filters it's three cache misses, against one for a blocked Bloom filter. However, since the reads are independent, the CPU can do them concurrently, so the checks are about as fast as with a Bloom filter.

Industry observers note that the filter uses the local wyhash3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh34 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks5, comparing unsure to xorfilter6 (binary fuse by the authors of the paper) and bloom (unsure's own Bloom filter) with 8-bit fingerprints (ns/op, lower is better):.

Memory, bits per item (lower is better):.

It has been revealed that unsure is the same size as xorfilter (same layout) with up to 25% faster checks. Compared to the Bloom filter, it uses up to 36% less memory, with checks as fast or faster, but up to 2.5× slower builds.

Recent findings suggest that ultraLogLog is a unique items counter that trades accuracy for space, like HyperLogLog7. It tells you approximately how many distinct items it has seen, no matter how many times each one appeared. UltraLogLog doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

UltraLogLog is a newer design (Otmar Ertl, 2024) that uses the space more efficiently: for the same error, it needs about 43% less memory than HyperLogLog. For example, a HyperLogLog sketch with 0.81% standard error takes 16 KB, while an UltraLogLog sketch with 0.86% error takes 8 KB. However, adding, counting, and merging are slower than with HyperLogLog.

UltraLogLog is useful in the same places as HyperLogLog: counting unique visitors, unique search queries, or distinct values in a database column, possibly across many machines or segments.

You can merge sketches to get the total number of unique items from all of them, without counting shared items twice.

The sketch has one setting: the precision p, which gives a relative standard error of 0.782/√(2^p). The default is p=13 with 0.86% error in 8 KB, close to the common HyperLogLog default (0.81% in 16 KB).

You can add items to a sketch, get the estimated count, and merge sketches. You cannot check if a specific item was added, remove items, or list them.

HyperLogLog hashes each item and uses the first p bits of the hash to pick one of m = 2^p registers. It calculates the rank (the number of leading zeros in the rest of the hash, plus one) and keeps the highest rank it has seen in the register. Seeing a rank of k suggests there were about 2^k items in the register. The count is estimated from all the registers together.

Industry observers note that A HyperLogLog register loses some information: it only keeps track of the highest value, not whether any slightly lower values were seen. These lower values show up at least as often as the highest one, so they can tell a lot about the count.

It has been revealed that ultraLogLog8 uses the registers more efficiently. Each register is still one byte, but it stores the highest rank k in the upper 6 bits, and whether k−1 and k−2 were seen in the lower 2 bits:.

Sources indicate that the count estimate uses the FGRA estimator from the UltraLogLog paper. Each register adds a weight based on its value, and the count is calculated as a power of the sum of the weights. Nearly empty and nearly full sketches get special handling, so the estimate stays accurate from zero to billions of items, without bias tables or a separate formula for small counts.

Unsure keeps a histogram of register values (256 four-byte counters, 1 KB) updated as the registers change. This way, Count reads the histogram instead of scanning all the registers. Merge checks 8 registers at a time using a few bitwise operations to find which ones the other sketch would change, and only updates those.

The item is hashed once with wyhash, and the 64-bit hash is split into the register index and the rank.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks9, comparing UltraLogLog to unsure's own HyperLogLog and axiom10 (HyperLogLog with LogLog-Beta estimator and sparse mode) (ns/op, lower is better):.

Accuracy and memory, relative RMSE over 1,000 sketches (lower is better):.

According to recent reports, ultraLogLog provides the same accuracy as HyperLogLog with almost half the memory. However, adding, counting, and merging are noticeably slower.

Recent findings suggest that hyperLogLog overview and how it works. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that ultraLogLog paper by Otmar Ertl, 2024. ↩︎.

axiomhq/hyperloglog by Axiom. ↩︎.

A log-linear histogram is a summary of a stream of numbers that trades accuracy for space. It can give you an approximate median, 99th percentile, or any other quantile of the data. It can also estimate what fraction of the numbers are below a certain value (the CDF). The histogram doesn't store the numbers, so it's much more compact than a sorted list.

For example, to find the exact 99th percentile of 1,000,000 response times, you'd have to keep all of them. With 64-bit floats, that takes 8 MB. A log-linear histogram estimates the same percentile within 0.39% of its true value using about 14 KB — almost 600 times less.

It has been revealed that the error is relative to the value: if the true 99th percentile is 200 ms, the histogram returns a value between 199.2 and 200.8 ms. This guarantee applies to every quantile, from the median to the most extreme outliers. The size of the histogram doesn't depend on the number of values, only on the accuracy you choose and on how wide the range of the values is.

A log-linear histogram is useful when you need percentiles for positive values that cover a wide range, like latencies, file sizes, or prices.

You can merge histograms to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, endpoint, or region). Merging is exact: a merged histogram is the same as if it had received all the values directly.

The histogram has two settings: relative error and value range. By default, the error is 0.0039 (0.39%) and the range is from 1e-9 to 1e18. Lowering the error or increasing the range uses more memory.

You can add numbers to a histogram, estimate quantiles and the CDF, and merge histograms. You cannot remove numbers or list them.

It has been revealed that A histogram splits the range of values into buckets and counts how many values are in each one. To estimate a quantile, it adds up the counts starting from the lowest bucket until it reaches the requested rank, then returns a value from that bucket. The accuracy of the estimate depends on how wide the bucket is.

With buckets that have equal widths, like 0–10, 10–20, and so on, every estimate has the same absolute error of ±5 around the bucket's midpoint. So the relative error is very large for small values and unnecessarily small for large values:.

A logarithmic histogram solves this by making each bucket's width proportional to its value. For example, if the bucket boundaries are powers of 1.02 (1, 1.02, 1.0404, ...), the end of each bucket is 2% larger than its start, so any value in the bucket is within about 1% of the bucket's midpoint. DDSketch11 uses this method. The downside is that finding the right bucket for a value means you have to calculate a logarithm, which is relatively slow.

A log-linear histogram gets almost the same result with cheaper math. First, it splits the values into ranges between powers of two: 1–2, 2–4, 4–8, and so on (these are called octaves). Then it splits every octave into the same number of equal-width buckets. For example, here are three octaves with 4 buckets each:.

It has been revealed that each octave is twice as long as the previous one, so its buckets are twice as wide, and the bucket width grows with the values, as in a logarithmic histogram. Finding the right bucket only takes a few bit operations instead of calculating a logarithm.

Sources indicate that hdrHistogram12 is the best-known log-linear histogram. It records integers: the position of the highest 1 bit of a number determines its octave, and the next few bits determine the bucket within the octave.

Unsure works with float64 numbers and finds the bucket in a similar way to HdrHistogram.

IEEE 754 double-precision format.

A float64 in Go (and most other languages) is made up of three parts:.

The number's value is 1.f × 2^e, where 1.f is a binary fraction between 1 and 2.

The exponent determines the octave, from 2^e to 2^(e+1). The top m bits of the mantissa determine one of the 2^m equal buckets within the octave.

For example, here's the number 5.25 with m=3 (8 buckets per octave). In binary, 5.25 = 1.0101₂ × 2², so the exponent is 2 (stored as 1025), and the mantissa starts with 0101:.

Industry observers note that add finds the bucket for the given number and increases the count. Merge adds the counts bucket by bucket. Quantile adds up the counts from the closer end (the leftmost bucket for q ≤ 0.5, the rightmost bucket otherwise) until it reaches the rank.

The number of mantissa bits m comes from the requested error: the constructor picks the smallest m for which the maximum error doesn't exceed the requested one. The default is m=7: 128 buckets per octave and an error of 0.39%.

A t-digest13 also estimates quantiles, but it limits the error in ranks: Quantile(0.99) returns a value whose rank is close to 99%. A log-linear histogram limits the error in values: Quantile(0.99) returns a value close to the true 99th percentile.

In the middle of the data, the two are pretty similar. But in a long tail, values at nearby ranks can be very different, so even a small error in rank can lead to a big difference in value. Here is the mean relative error of an 8.5 KB t-digest (δ=100) on 1M values from three distributions: lognormal (as in the benchmarks), Pareto with α=1.5 (a longer tail), and uniform between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 (no tail):.

A log-linear histogram of about the same size (1% error, 8 KB) has an error below 0.78% for all these cases.

In a recent development, so a log-linear histogram is better for latencies, sizes, and other positive measurements with long tails. A t-digest is better when you need a fixed size no matter what the values are, or when the values can be arbitrarily close to zero.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks14, comparing unsure to hdr15 (log-linear, integers only, fixed range) and dd16 (DDSketch, logarithmic buckets) with a lognormal distribution (ns/op, lower is better):.

Mean relative error at the requested 0.1%, over 1M values (lower is better):.

Memory after adding 1M values (lower is better):.

According to recent reports, unsure adds values as fast as hdr and 5× faster than dd, queries 5–19× faster than hdr and about 35× faster than dd, and merges about as fast as dd and 35–175× faster than hdr. It's slightly less accurate than hdr (using 5× less memory), and more accurate than dd (using 1.4× more memory).

Industry observers note that DDSketch paper by Charles Masson et al., 2019. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that T-digest overview and how it works. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, log-linear histogram benchmarks. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that hdrHistogram/hdrhistogram-go by Coda Hale. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that dataDog/sketches-go by Datadog. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that minHash estimates how similar two sets are. It summarizes each set in a short fixed-size signature (for example, 256 numbers). Comparing two signatures gives the approximate Jaccard similarity of the sets: |A∩B| / |A∪B|, the proportion of unique items that both sets share.

Recent findings suggest that the size of a signature doesn't depend on the size of the set, so you can compare two sets of a million items each just by comparing 256 pairs of numbers instead of checking every item. Plus, each set's signature is only calculated once, so comparing lots of sets to each other is relatively cheap.

According to recent reports, minHash is useful for finding near-duplicate documents, like web pages or essays (represented as sets of words or 3-word phrases). It's also useful for finding similar user profiles (as sets of liked items) or overlapping datasets (as sets of keys).

In a recent development, the MinHash sketch has one setting: the signature size k, which gives a standard error of √(J(1−J)/k) for true similarity J. For example, with k=256 and J=0.5:.

It has been revealed that you can add items to a sketch, merge sketches, and get and compare signatures. You cannot check if a specific item was added, count the items, remove them, or list them.

Recent findings suggest that classic MinHash17 hashes every item with k different hash functions. Here are two sets, A = {fox, cat, dog, owl} and B = {fox, dog, emu}, and their item hashes for k=4:.

Sources indicate that for each hash function, the set keeps only the smallest hash value among its items. These k minimums are the set's signature. To estimate the similarity of two sets, compare their signatures position by position, count the number of equal values, and divide by k:.

Sources indicate that the estimated similarity (0.5) is different from the actual value (2 shared items / 5 distinct items = 0.4). To get a more accurate estimate, k is usually much larger than in this example.

Sources indicate that one permutation hashing18 hashes every item once, with a single hash function, and splits the range of hash values into k equal buckets. Each bucket keeps the smallest hash value among its items. Here are the same sets with k=4, using h1 from above:.

It has been revealed that each bucket works like a separate MinHash over the items in its range. So the bucket minimums form a signature, and comparing two signatures works the same way. But there is a catch: when a set isn't much larger than k, some buckets end up empty (shown as · above), so there's nothing to compare in them.

According to recent reports, optimal densification19 solves this by filling each empty bucket with the value from another bucket in the same set. Each empty bucket tries other buckets in a pseudo-random order and copies the value of the first non-empty one:.

This order depends only on the empty bucket's position, so two similar sets tend to fill empty spots with the same values. This makes the estimate work for sets of any size, with about the same error as classic MinHash.

Unsure keeps the k bucket minimums in the sketch. Add and Merge use the original buckets. Densification only happens in Signature, and it makes a copy of the buckets without modifying the sketch.

In a recent development, each item is hashed once with 64-bit wyhash. Multiplying the hash by k once gives both the bucket and the value to store:.

Densification fills empty buckets in a coordinated way, spreading the copies evenly across the non-empty buckets. This keeps the error close to classic MinHash, and makes densification fast even for small sets.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks20, comparing unsure to dgryski21 (classic MinHash) (ns/op, lower is better):.

RMSE of the similarity estimate at k=256 and J=0.5 (lower is better):.

Unsure adds items 6–70× faster than dgryski, compares signatures at the same speed, has roughly the same accuracy, and uses half the memory.

Sources indicate that classic MinHash paper by Andrei Broder, 1997. ↩︎.

In a recent development, one permutation hashing by Ping Li et al., 2012. ↩︎.

Optimal densification paper by Anshumali Shrivastava, 2017. ↩︎.

In a recent development, dgryski/go-minhash by Damian Gryski. ↩︎.

Tech Report: Welcome RL Environments to the hub

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the newly introduced RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the newly introduced RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

It has been revealed that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

It has been revealed that framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Industry observers note that harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer highlights the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

Industry observers note that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

According to recent reports, the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

Recent findings suggest that that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

It has been revealed that we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment indicates up in the filter.

It has been revealed that the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

In a recent development, if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.
