📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

Sources indicate that I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

Sources indicate that headlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough highlights a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

In a recent development, what I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

In a recent development, AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s debuts Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus intends in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

In a recent development, amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – Latest Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Sources indicate that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • These arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Sources indicate that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

These arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

Industry observers note that while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Sources indicate that importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

It has been revealed that the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is vital for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

It has been revealed that we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Complications and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

Sources indicate that the check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Recent findings suggest that open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as newly introduced TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and consumers better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

Latest Update: How I Got Postgres into a Single Binary

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies.
  • At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres.
  • In a recent development, SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies. It's a full SQL database, designed as an embeddable library, that stores all its data in a single file. The sqlite3 command line tool is great too. You point it at a file and run queries. There's no server to run.

At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres. It's the most capable general purpose SQL database, trusted in production at scale, and is something of an industry standard. With that comes complexity, starting with the fact that it's client-server.

In a recent development, SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally. These applications can use SQLite and manage it themselves, so you barely know there's a database involved.

Industry observers note that so when you find self-hostable open source software you'd like to run on your own computer, it can be daunting when it says it requires Postgres. Now you're responsible for setting up a database and getting it ready for the software to use.

Sources indicate that sure, you can run Postgres in Docker, and plenty of projects recommend it. But now you have two dependencies. If you don't already have Docker, you have to install it, which can mean a VM and a daemon on your machine. Then you have to run Postgres in it and make sure it's running whenever you use the software. That's a lot just to try something you don't know you want yet.

Wouldn't it be great to have the SQLite experience, but with Postgres?

That's miniPG . It isn't Postgres as a library. There's already a WASM project for that, reasonably called PGlite. miniPG is closer to the SQLite CLI: a single program that embeds a full Postgres server and client, wrapped up so you can use it the way you'd use sqlite3. Point it at a path, that path becomes the database, and you can run queries against it right away. There's no server to set up or keep running.

Jumping into a newly introduced Postgres database to try something out or debug it is now easier than using Postgres in a Docker container, and you don't need Docker at all. And miniPG still provides a fully functional Postgres server for software that needs one. In many cases, you can just launch an open source program that looks for its Postgres config in the environment with miniPG.

Industry observers note that miniPG comes as a single, self-contained executable. You can just point it at a directory and run a query. There's no server to start, nothing to configure, and the result comes back immediately.

According to recent reports, that directory is the database. When nothing is using it, it's just files on disk. You can copy it, back it up, or delete it.

This is actually real Postgres, not a compatibility layer, and this binary compiles to Mac, Windows, and Linux.

When some software expects a Postgres server, miniPG can be one:.

Like I mentioned before, it can even launch programs with environment variables that configure it for this Postgres database:.

It has been revealed that when the program is terminated, there's no database daemon to leave around or remember to stop. Only the data itself is kept right there on disk, ready to be used next time.

Instructions for getting it and even an interactive demo are available on the miniPG website .

Software people, from developers to open source power users, and agents too, can use miniPG whenever they'd reach for SQLite but need Postgres.

This really makes Postgres more viable for scenarios it wasn't before. I'd love to hear the use cases I haven't thought of.

miniPG is the result of several attempts at embedding real Postgres into a standalone, cross platform binary.

In a recent development, the obvious place to start was PGlite. The name indicates it all, and in a sense it delivers: it's Postgres compiled to WebAssembly. In Go, you can load the module with the wazero runtime, run Postgres inside your program, and have your app connect to it. That's very close to the SQLite library experience.

Brad Fitzpatrick even made a proof of concept that does this in a way that makes PGlite work as a driver for the standard Go SQL package.

The catch is that PGlite only supports a single connection and a single session. Software written for a real Postgres server often assumes it can have more. A common pattern is to start a transaction, then make another query on a separate connection before committing. With only one connection, that second query waits for a transaction that's waiting on it. The app I was trying to run deadlocked.

If I needed real Postgres, I could run real Postgres in a virtual machine I could embed. I have a soft spot for using webviews as portable containers, so I ran v86, an x86 emulator for the browser, inside one, and booted a full Postgres server in it.

Industry observers note that the rest was plumbing. The headless webview opens a WebSocket back to the host program. Postgres connections are tunneled through it, and Postgres writes its data to a mount served over the same socket. The benefit of this approach is whatever platform the host program runs on, Postgres is always the same build running in the same VM.

I even built webframe for this, a library and CLI for running a native system webview headlessly.

In a recent development, the result was a proof of concept I called postgres-standalone: one binary, any platform, give it a port and a data directory, and you get a full Postgres server. It worked!

Sources indicate that however, it was also an order of magnitude slower than native. Postgres in a VM in WebAssembly in a browser. Initializing and checking a database took a while. In the best case, on my M3 MacBook, it took 7 seconds before it would accept a connection.

Sources indicate that I'd already written a design doc for the SQLite-style CLI: give it a directory, run a query, no server to run. On this stack, though, every SELECT * would sit there for 7 seconds first. That ruins the experience, so I had to shelve it. I had proven that embeddable Postgres was possible, just not pleasant.

Later, for unrelated reasons, I built Hyper9 . Inspired by system API translation, an approach that Wine and Valve's Proton are built on, combined with a unique way to use hypervisors, Hyper9 lets you run Proposal 9 executables at near native speed on all platforms.

I'll be posting more about Plan 9 soon, but with a little extra magic, I was able to run the same Postgres at near native speed, in isolation, on all platforms. It's effectively the same approach as the previous attempt, but now without the slowdown.

Industry observers note that startup went from 7 seconds to 800ms. So I dusted off the design doc and built it. PGlite was taken, so postgres-standalone became miniPG.

miniPG isn't a replacement for real Postgres deployments. If you're running in the cloud, using replicas, or serving many owners over many connections, use Postgres the normal way.

miniPG is for local, single-user programs: the places SQLite would fit, but you need Postgres.

That said, go ahead and see how far you can push it!

I'd really like to see how miniPG holds up in the wild, especially across different platforms and architectures. Please try it and tell me what breaks.

It has been revealed that if this works, it proves a model that goes well beyond Postgres: taking complicated systems and packaging them as a single binary for more specific use cases. That's the part I find most exciting, and it's one of many upcoming possibilities Hyper9 enables.

Once a month I send out a newsletter with a little of everything: newly introduced articles, the best of the logs, useful resources, and a few surprises.

Nvidia’s journey to forge the one CPU SKU to rule them all

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of newly introduced SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between.
  • But if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill.
  • According to recent reports, nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Each generation of Intel Xeons or AMD Epycs brings dozens of newly introduced SKUs: high-core count parts tuned for throughput, high-frequency ones optimized for latency, low-power chips designed for the edge, and everything in between.

But if you ask Ian Finder, who heads development of Nvidia’s datacenter CPUs, for the vast majority of use cases, all those SKUs are overkill. “There was sort of an overskewing, for many years on the other vendors side of things,” he told El Reg on the sidelines of Supercomputing 2026 this week.

According to recent reports, nvidia is a relative newcomer to the datacenter CPU space. The company’s first part, called Grace, rolled out in 2023, but didn’t see widespread deployment outside AI headnodes, high-end NICs, and a handful of standalone CPU deployments by hyperscalers like Meta.

According to recent reports, we explored the chip in greater detail earlier this year, but the GPU slinger’s latest CPU, Vera, is a different beast. In addition to showing up as part of Nvidia’s Vera-Rubin superchips, the CPU will also be offered in standalone CPU racks, storage, and context memory systems. Just this week, Nvidia declared a latest rack with 192 Vera CPUs aimed at high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, which don’t translate well to GPUs. And at least on paper, a single SKU with 88 cores clocking to 3.3 GHz powers all of them.

Historically, CPUs with different combinations of cores, clocks, I/O, and power have been used in these roles.

According to Finder, most datacenter CPUs haven’t been loaded that heavily, and as a result unloaded latency has been the optimization point. As a consequence, CPUs that rely on high core counts to boost throughput often suffer from elevated loaded latencies.

On the flip side, chipmakers can optimize for loaded latency, but this usually comes at the expense of throughput. We see this pretty clearly across AMD’s last few generations of Epycs, where it designed both space-efficient Zen-C cores that prioritize throughput and fatter frequency-optimized versions that prioritize latency.

Industry observers note that “As more cores are up and running, your latency to memory gets higher because you have to deal with congestion on the connectivity buses,” More than Moore analyst Ian Cutress tells The Reg. “What Nvidia is saying is right. Sometimes, you do have to pick between core count and core latency.”.

88 custom cores, 176 funky threads, 1.5 TB of laptop RAM, and 1.8 TB/s of NVLink connectivity — this isn't your typical datacenter chip.

It has been revealed that with Vera, Nvidia sought to thread that needle to design a balanced architecture that maintains low latencies and high throughput even when all 88 cores are loaded. This does mean making some compromises – in particular, the CPU's vector unit isn’t the beefiest. But if you’ve got GPUs capable of running vectorized code, that compromise starts to make a lot more sense – and if you’re buying Vera you almost certainly do.

“If you do a few things like that, you can actually get a part that, for the workloads people care about — knowledge agents for CI/CD, for software engineering, or databases and analytics — you can build a part that gets you the same performance per core as the frequency-optimized x86 parts at the same throughput per watt as the density-optimized parts,” Finder argued.

Industry observers note that we should note that Nvidia isn’t unique in this line of thinking. Cloud providers have long passed on the highest core-count parts in Intel or AMD’s lineup in favor of parts they feel deliver the right mix of throughput, latency, memory bandwidth, and capacity.

The reason, in part, is that cloud providers don’t know exactly what their customers will actually be doing with those cores, and so it’s better to offer something that’s well-rounded than one that has the highest clocks or lowest latency. This same logic works pretty well for agent sandboxes.

“Nvidia is confident that it understands the market well enough that one chip will cover most use cases,” Cutress stated. “You could argue that Nvidia just wants to corner that bulk market.”.

Having mentioned that, there are plenty of reasons to have multiple SKUs or product lines. Throughout much of AMD’s latest launch cycle, the House of Zen has argued its chips make for better agentic CPUs because agents aren’t one workload but many. Some may benefit from higher core counts while others may benefit from higher frequency, and AMD’s more diverse portfolio offers choice.

To that point, Vera does have one trick up its sleeve: a split personality. The processor is one of the few Arm chips that supports simultaneous multithreading (SMT), but the way it works differs wildly from what Intel would call Hyperthreading.

When enabled, SMT effectively bifurcates Vera’s Olympus cores. Eighty-eight cores turns into something that functionally looks more like 176 narrower cores. So if you need more throughput than 88 cores afford, or your workload doesn’t benefit materially from a wider core, Vera does offer some flexibility.

According to recent reports, 16 channels of DDR5, 5 GHz clock speeds, and support for CXL 3.1 memory god boxes? What's not to like?

According to recent reports, A broader SKU stack also helps with binning. Chip manufacturing isn’t a perfect process, and you’re going to run into defective cores from time to time. Binning allows chipmakers to sell these defective chips at a discount.

Cutress suspects that Nvidia is probably doing this for its customers and it’s just not advertising them as different SKUs the way Intel and AMD have the past few decades.

For instance, a hyperscaler might be happy to take a 72-core variant of Vera that clocks a little higher or delivers more memory bandwidth per core for the same amount of power.

But for now we have just the one, for the green lord on their green throne in the land of AI where the bots lie. ®.

#138162. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2038 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • Sources indicate that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

Sources indicate that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Industry observers note that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

Industry observers note that the user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Sources indicate that realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

In a recent development, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

It has been revealed that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

It has been revealed that consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Sources indicate that completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into latest executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

It has been revealed that autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Industry observers note that identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates newly introduced tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a latest target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

Recent findings suggest that the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

According to recent reports, to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Industry observers note that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

It has been revealed that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Sources indicate that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

Industry observers note that the pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

In a recent development, for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Recent findings suggest that failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Industry observers note that passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

Industry observers note that A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

In a recent development, after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We initiative to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

According to recent reports, we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

Industry observers note that we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Industry observers note that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates latest tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

#138161. Industry News: AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2070 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI).
  • Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless.
  • GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:.

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

It has been revealed that GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

According to recent reports, let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console indicates the upcoming capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

It has been revealed that next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:.

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview demonstrates what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

It has been revealed that functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Recent findings suggest that four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

Sources indicate that that’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I enhancement MODEL_ID and publish a upcoming version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

Recent findings suggest that for production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab highlights the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

It has been revealed that skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

It has been revealed that serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Industry observers note that capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

According to recent reports, large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

It has been revealed that see GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

Industry observers note that after invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Prepares and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers.
  • Sources indicate that if you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer.
  • According to recent reports, tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers.

Sources indicate that if you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge.

According to recent reports, tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES. He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too.

It’s not a major model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model.

Sources indicate that there are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference.

Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an glitch given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB.

Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all.

In a recent development, “It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.”.

If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above.

If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge.

“The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.”.

That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun.

“ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edwards told us.

While a human may have designed the experiment, the coding work was done by AI, Edwards told us – he’s been interested in it since the 1990s and is pursuing more experiments with tiny AI models using the help of the bigger ones.

Industry observers note that “I've been theorizing about what I call ‘tiny talking machines’ … over the past year,” Edwards told us, and he’s been able to use coding agents to turn those ideas into actual software. ChatGPT for SNES is one example, and he also created an NES ROM called Séance that uses an even smaller AI model able to run on an original Nintendo Entertainment System that simulates talking to a ghost in a haunted game cartridge.

Industry observers note that “I designed the scope of what the software should be, how it should work broadly, what chip it should use, how the interface should look and work, and the sounds it makes when it types responses,” Edwards told us. He added that he sees the project as an AI/human collaboration, which is where he believes AI works best.

Recent findings suggest that “The AI agents who did the coding for this project right now advise that we've hit the limit of how good the AI model can be on the limited hardware,” Edwards remarked - he’s not taking their word for it, though. “It's up to human creativity to transcend those assumptions. I have already come up with fresh ideas that I believe can make a tiny model like ChatGPT for SNES even more coherent, and I'm working on them now.” ®.

#138157. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2618 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Sources indicate that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Industry observers note that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Sources indicate that two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

Recent findings suggest that that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

It has been revealed that final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

In a recent development, an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

It has been revealed that starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

According to recent reports, table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

It has been revealed that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

It has been revealed that kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

According to recent reports, claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Recent findings suggest that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Recent findings suggest that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Industry observers note that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

Recent findings suggest that this is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

Sources indicate that A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

In a recent development, the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

In a recent development, table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

It has been revealed that none of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

Recent findings suggest that we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

According to recent reports, classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

It has been revealed that thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

According to recent reports, each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

It has been revealed that gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Recent findings suggest that now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

Sources indicate that the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

It has been revealed that ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

This small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.
