PLUS: Lenovo's infra group finally makes big profit; Indonesia’s glaciers are gone; Australian bank releases its AI bug-finder; and more!

Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens.

That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control.

Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI.

The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.”.

Recent findings suggest that “CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.”.

The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1.

The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar.

It has been revealed that “CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.”.

Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hyperscalers.

The AI boom has finally done what various strategy shifts and waves of hype could not: propel the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) to a $1 billion quarterly profit.

In its Q2 results announcement [PDF] last week, the manufacturer revealed ISG revenue hit a quarterly record of $11.3 billion, up 178 percent year-over-year, and that lovely big profit. At a time when enterprise hardware supply chains are tight, Lenovo notes it was able to increase shipments of x86 servers and even emerge as the largest vendor of such systems with 16 percent market share.

Sources indicate that lenovo also claimed it’s moved further ahead as the planet’s premier PC provider, by pointing to 15 percent year-on-year growth for its intelligent devices group where quarterly revenue reached $17.4 billion. The manufacturer claims it has 23.8 percent of the PC market and now has seven percent more market share than its closest rival, Apple. The company said premium devices account for 63 percent of its PC business.

Overall revenue rose 48 percent year over year to $30.24 billion for the quarter.

It may surprise readers to know that Indonesia, the nation that spreads across 17,000 islands in the tropical latitudes of 11°S to 6°N, is home to alpine regions sufficiently high that glaciers can form.

Indonesia’s glaciers clung to the top of Puncak Jaya, aka Carstenz Pyramid, a 4,884-meter peak on New Guinea at 4°S.

Sadly, an assessment published last week by NASA says the glaciers have probably melted to the point at which not much is left other than a few patches of ice.

Industry observers note that NASA last week posted images that show glaciers covering 4.31 km2 atop Puncak Jaya in 1988, and another from this year that indicates most of that ice is gone. Images from September 2025 apparently demonstrated just .09km2 of ice remained.

Sources indicate that “To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts,” NASA’s Kathryn Hansen wrote. “Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.”.

For what it’s worth, commercial operators run expeditions to Puncak Jaya. Peak-baggers seek it out because some consider it the highest mountain in Australasia/Oceania and therefore one of the “Seven Summits” –  the highest point on each continent.

The Reg won’t get into the debate about the validity of including Puncak Jaya on that list, but if you fancy some equatorial alpine action your correspondent recently climbed Malaysia’s 4,095m Mount Kinabalu. It’s an overnight walk that requires no technical skills or gear, but definitely demands supple knees. The peak was clearly glaciated in the distant past but snow is now extremely rare on Kinabalu.

Here’s an odd one: Australia’s Commonwealth Bank (CBA) created an AI-powered tool to scan its bespoke code for bugs, and has now packaged it as a free release called “CodeCheck.”.

The bank indicates analyzes the output of OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code with “a consistent process for analyzing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers.” Apparently, it is “ based on an approach used within CBA, but it is not the same as, and does not represent, the systems, tools or controls CBA uses internally.”.

The bank posted CodeCheck to GitHub, where it warns the project is “a one-time open-source release for businesses to evaluate” and that it will not actively maintain, update, or support the code.

Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) last week announced it has reached an agreement with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) to take over responsibility for running rolls out of its flagship H3 rocket when used in certain configurations.

The deal means MHI will handle releases for H3s that use a pair of LE-9 liquid-fuel engines alongside two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters.

JAXA will continue running launches that use different, or experimental, configurations.

Once JAXA is satisfied those newly introduced rigs are reliable, it looks to transition them to private operators, too. ®.

Article: Building Reliability into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover.
  • Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.
  • Industry observers note that I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover.

Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.

Industry observers note that I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title. The conditions were all there. I just hadn't looked at them as a system that would eventually fail, only as infrastructure that had been working fine so far. My team owned a Terraform execution platform. The registry was backed by S3, which is standard stuff. Nothing else exotic was added. One morning the dashboard lit up, showing registry failures and artifacts not downloading. We declared an incident and started the usual process of elimination.

In a recent development, two hours into our investigation, I was still convinced we had done something wrong. Perhaps we had a misconfigured bucket policy or added a permissions boundary incorrectly. Hopefully, this problem was  embarrassingly fixable. I kept going back to our changes, our config, and our code. The problem wasn't in any of those places.

Sources indicate that the actual cause took hours to surface. S3 signed URLs worked fine. You could manually call one and download an artifact without issue. But Terraform calls those URLs in sequence. When it resolves module dependencies, it fires a bunch of them back-to-back. Some of those requests were silently failing. Not all of them failed and not  in any consistent pattern, just... some, which was enough, to break the pipeline. From every dashboard we viewed, it looked like a registry bug, rather than an S3 bug.

In a recent development, december 15–16, 2026. Examine how senior practitioners run agents, evals, model serving, and AI-assisted engineering in production, including what failed and what changed. Register Now.

Industry observers note that we found the real cause by building a controlled test environment on my laptop. The failures were intermittent and appeared only in production, where experimenting is discouraged, so I needed a safe way to reproduce them. I wrote a small Terraform configuration that downloads modules from our registry, the same path our pipelines use, and ran it under a load test. I also checked out the Terraform source and added logging for HTTP request and response headers. Logging exposed an easy-to-miss detail. Terraform hands module downloads to HashiCorp's go-getter library, which sends a HEAD request to each signed URL before the GET, to check whether the download can be resumed. The load test reproduced the failure within ten minutes; the logs traced it to that HEAD request rather than to our registry. I proposed that a recent change in how AWS handled the HEAD request was producing the downstream 404.

This hypothesis was initially not obvious even to their support personnel. I substantiated it with clear reproduction steps and diagnostic evidence. After they escalated internally to their architecture team, they confirmed that a recent change in request handling was the root cause and rolled back the change, restoring expected behavior. The lesson I took from this situation was when a managed dependency fails intermittently, reproduce your client's exact call pattern outside of production and instrument the client, not just the server.

Industry observers note that detection took a few hours. Recovery took nearly twenty-four hours, most of which was spent on support calls proving the matter was on their end waiting for AWS to acknowledge other customers were affected and waiting for the rollback to ship. Once AWS rolled back the S3 deployment, concurrent signed URL requests stabilized and the registry recovered without any changes on our end.

The mechanism here, signed URLs, concurrency, isn't the key part. The important part is the assumption I had been running on without examining it, that cloud infrastructure is reliable by default. That 99.99 percent is essentially "always works". I had treated the SLA like a guarantee rather than a statistical claim about a distribution with a tail I just hadn't seen yet.

Fifty-two minutes and thirty-six seconds of downtime per year. Considering the scale at which we were operating, hitting that window was not a matter of if, because I already had and more than once. I just hadn't treated it as evidence that my design needed to change.

Every organization I have worked for has made the same mistake and I bet that yours has too. Someone builds an observability system early on. They care about it. The dashboards are thoughtful, the alerts are calibrated, and the runbooks are linked. Then the system grows, engineers move on, haphazardly adding and wiring  in upcoming services without anyone updating what came before. The people who built the original dashboards aren't around to update them and the people who are around are nervous to touch something they didn't build and don't fully understand. Alerts drift out of calibration and dashboards start showing challenges nobody on the current team knows how to interpret.

Sources indicate that then something breaks at a bad hour and the person on call opens Grafana and spends twenty minutes just trying to figure out what they are seeing. I have been in that position. The problem runs deeper than knowledge. It is a design failure, not a skills gap. The dashboards were built as a reporting layer, something that shows you what is happening. But they were never connected to anything that does something about what is happening. The human is still the bridge between signal and response.

Industry observers note that the mistake has nothing to do with tooling choice, query language, or dashboard layout. The mistake is treating observability as a way to inform humans rather than a way to drive system behavior. The difference is significant in practice. In reporting, a human receives an alert, interprets it under stress at a bad hour, decides what to do, and acts. In a control plane, the system receives and evaluates the signal against a defined policy, acts, and tells the human what happened. One of those scales with your headcount and on-call rotation, while the other breaks the moment both are stretched thin.

Recent findings suggest that none of the tooling required for this design is new. Prometheus has had alerting rules and webhook routing for years. Terraform can reconfigure routing weights. The components all exist; they just haven't been wired together with automation as the explicit goal. The pattern is the same at every scale, from pod autoscaling to regional failover: observe, decide, act, and confirm.

In a recent development, I have run Prometheus and Grafana stacks across hundreds of services, large builds and deployment pipelines, with thousands of executions per day. These tools are powerful but carry an operational cost teams consistently underestimate. Consider that expertise concentrates. When the person who really knows the stack leaves, calibration drifts silently until something breaks at the worst possible moment. Treat your observability stack with the same ownership model as your production services with regular reviews, real failure testing, and collective ownership that does not expire when the original author leaves.

Figure 1. Observability as a reporting layer vs. a control plane.The difference is whether a human or the system bridges signal to response. (Source: created by author.).

I have never worked with anyone who needed a whitepaper to understand why multi-region matters. Instead, they needed an outage. After a major regional failure hit one of our cloud providers, the conversation about moving the Terraform registry to active-active architecture happened. The registry is called during every pipeline execution: every build, every deployment, and every release. When it goes down, every build, every deployment, and every release across every team stops with it. The blast radius of that dependency is much larger than it looks on an architecture diagram; it took a real outage for that to land viscerally for everyone involved.

Industry observers note that we chose active-active, not active-passive. The reason for this choice comes up less often in architecture discussions than it should. We wanted the secondary region under real production load before we needed it for failover.

Active-passive looks good in diagrams. The failure mode is subtle and tends to surface at the worst possible time. The passive region has never handled your actual traffic. Its configuration has drifted unnoticed. Caches are cold and downstream dependencies haven't been exercised under anything close to real load. You have tested it in staging, maybe, with synthetic load that doesn't match your real traffic profile. When you fail under pressure, during an active incident with people watching, you discover all of these challenges simultaneously.

Sources indicate that I have been on that incident bridge. It is a specific kind of unpleasantry. You are trying to recover from one problem while discovering a second set of problems you didn't know you had. Active-active costs more. You have to keep regions in sync. Data consistency under partition requires careful thought. But when a region degrades, you shift load in a system that has been running in two regions all along, not making a leap of faith into an untested environment. We ran 50/50 under normal operation, which gave us continuous validation. Both regions were exercised constantly under real load. But 50/50 is the steady state, not the failure state. When a region actually degrades, traffic shifts to 100/0.

Industry observers note that that transition is what you are building toward and it has to be tested deliberately. We ran chaos testing specifically for this situation. Cut one region entirely, verify the other absorbs full load cleanly, and confirm recovery when it comes back. If you haven't tested the 100/0 state, you haven't tested your disaster recovery (DR) system. Instead, you have tested your routing config. Multi-region is expensive to build and maintain. For a critical build-time dependency like this registry, it was the right call. But it should be a deliberate decision, not a default assumption.

Sources indicate that two failure modes in this design are worth being honest about, because neither demonstrates up in a clean chaos test. The first is a failure that is not regional at all. The S3 incident hit both regions at the same time, because both depended on the same S3 behavior. Regional failover cannot fix that problem. Failover shifts traffic to the other region, which is failing the same way, so failover triggers there too and traffic shifts back. The automation keeps moving traffic between two broken regions and adds noise to an incident it cannot resolve. Route 53 behaves the same way at the DNS layer. When every weighted record is unhealthy, it returns all of them rather than none. When both regions degrade together, the cause is a shared dependency. The correct automated response is to hold traffic where it is and page a human.

The second failure mode is a health check that reports the wrong thing. Our /health endpoint confirmed that the application process was running, not that it could do its job. If the backend database in one region goes down, the application keeps answering /health with 200 OK while real requests fail. This is exactly the case for which regional failover exists, but Route 53 sees a healthy endpoint and keeps sending traffic to the broken region. The confirmation Lambda checks the same endpoint, so it would also report a failover into that region as successful. A health check has to exercise the functionality the service delivers, such as a lightweight database read, not just confirm the process is up. Deep checks carry their own risk. If the dependency they test is shared by both regions, they bring back the first failure mode.

It has been revealed that DNS TTL is the single most common DR misconfiguration I have seen in otherwise well-designed systems and it is worth addressing directly. TTL controls how long a resolver caches a DNS record before requerying. If the setting is too high (e.g.,  three hundred seconds, six hundred seconds, or whatever the module default happened to be) and your failover logic can fire correctly, then your routing weights can update correctly and clients will keep hitting the degraded region for minutes because their resolvers haven't expired the old record. The failover executed correctly, but the traffic never moved because resolvers were still serving the cached record.

It has been revealed that if the setting is too low, then you have built an overreactive system. A transient latency spike triggers a DNS change. The concern resolves thirty seconds later. Now you have regions flip-flopping and amplifying instability that would have cleared on their own. The right TTL is a deliberate number, chosen against your RTO, your health check interval, and your false positive tolerance. Most teams are running whatever default Infrastructure as code (IaC) module was set years ago. They don't know what that number is until they are debugging a failover that didn't go the way they expected.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. DNS TTL and failover timing. A weight change that fires correctly can still leave traffic stranded in the degraded region until resolver caches expire. (Source: created by author.).

Sources indicate that what separates DR systems that actually work from those existing only on paper is automation with confirmation, not just detecting failure, but acting on it and verifying the action succeeded. Most teams that have invested seriously in DR have detection, such as alerts that fire when error rates spike or health checks fail. Fewer have built the response layer, the automated action that runs when the signal fires. Fewer still have built the confirmation layer, the part checking whether or not the response actually worked.

This last piece matters more than people realize. Automated failover without confirmation is a system taking an action and then going quiet. Did the secondary region receive the traffic? Did DNS propagate before the TTL window? Are the downstream dependencies there responding correctly? A system capable of answering these questions by continuing to observe after acting is one you can trust. A system that only fires and then goes silent is an untested hypothesis.

According to recent reports, the pattern looks like this in practice: A Prometheus alerting rule evaluates a composite signal, error rate above threshold AND p99 latency elevated AND sustained for a defined window. This observation is crucial. Single-metric alerts are noisy. A transient spike fires them constantly for things that resolve on their own in a minute or two. The composite condition with a duration requirement indicates you only trigger degradation that has actually persisted.

Most implementations stop at the alert. Here the alert is the entry point to an automated chain. How traffic moves depends on the topology. In an active-active setup, Route 53 does the switching. Each regional record carries a weight and a health check. When a region's health check fails, Route 53 stops returning that record, so traffic shifts to the healthy region with no custom code. In an active-passive setup, the alert drives the switch. Alertmanager routes it to a webhook, which invokes a Lambda function that flips the Route 53 failover record to the secondary region. In both cases, the alert also triggers a confirmation Lambda that polls the target region's health endpoint until it confirms the region is returning healthy responses. The human receives a notification only after the Lambda confirms the loop completed successfully. Detection, action, and confirmation form one connected loop. Observability drives the action and then verifies the outcome.

According to recent reports, figure 3. The detect–act–confirm loop. Prometheus fires, Route 53 shifts traffic, Lambda polls until the target region confirms healthy, then notifies the team. (Source: created by author.).

That confirmation loop, in practice, looks like this:.

Recent findings suggest that the loop does not close until the health check returns 200. If it never does, the function returns unconfirmed and that signal itself becomes an alert, not a silent failure.

Industry observers note that this is a Terraform configuration for the Route 53 side. Both regions carry equal weight and Route 53 stops returning a region's record when its health check fails:.

The by (region) clause is what makes this rule region-aware. It evaluates the composite signal independently per region, so when one region degrades while the other remains healthy, the alert fires with the specific region label that tells the automation exactly which region is degraded.

The for: 90s is doing real work there. Without it, this alert fires on blips. With it, the alert fires only when something has been consistently degraded for a minute and a half, which is a meaningfully different situation.

Finally, there is testing. The most effective practice I know for thorough testing is the game day,  a scheduled exercise where the team deliberately injects real failures into production systems and works through detection, response, and recovery in real time, with the people who would handle a real incident in the room. It is not a runbook walk-through in staging.

Game days find the human gaps as reliably as they find technical ones. Who actually has decision authority when you cannot reach the incident commander? Where is the runbook for this failure mode, exactly? Does everyone know? The first time most teams run one, the answer to these questions is uncomfortable. That is the point. Finding it during a game day costs an afternoon.

Sources indicate that the validation that teams most consistently skip is testing that the confirmation layer correctly recognizes a successful failover and stops taking action. People test that the failover fires. They rarely test what happens if it fires and the system thinks it didn't work. That is a real path to cascading failures you created yourself.

Recent findings suggest that the S3 incident wasn't something I had modeled. Nobody had a runbook for "S3 silently breaks concurrent signed URL requests under load following an internal deployment". The assumption that underpins a lot of how we build systems, that the infrastructure below us is basically reliable, is fine most of the time, which is exactly why it is so rarely questioned.

Three steps will turn your failover plan into a working system. First, pick one alert that pages a human today and wire it to an automated response with a confirmation step. Second, put your secondary region under real production traffic before you need it for failover. Third, on your next game day, test the confirmation layer, not just the trigger. Verify that the system recognizes a successful failover and stops acting. If you haven't validated all three, you have a plan, not a system.

Infrastructure will fail, and the next failure will probably be one you haven't seen before. Whether a person has to piece together a response manually or the system handles it was decided long before the incident started.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.
  • It has been revealed that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard.
  • According to recent reports, JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.

It has been revealed that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file quickly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to patch it, and then forget to do so later.

According to recent reports, JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits?

Pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change.

I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around.

TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make new empty commits on top of other empty commits.

In a recent development, I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this.

Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.

#138132. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2999 w)
📖 Baca

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Industry observers note that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Industry observers note that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post demonstrates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that intends, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

According to recent reports, the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

According to recent reports, the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

It has been revealed that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:.

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

This is a substantial model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/fresh/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

Industry observers note that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: the Future of Apache Iceberg.
  • Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.
  • Apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: the Future of Apache Iceberg.

Nov 20, 2026 3 min read.

Apache Iceberg V4 proposes a redesign of table metadata to improve scalability and support more frequent writes, alongside new capabilities for data management and schema evolution. Daniel Weeks, co-creator of Apache Iceberg and member of technical staff at Databricks, presented a session at QCon San Francisco on the fourth version of the Apache Iceberg open table format specification.

Iceberg V4 will address the limitations of managing very large tables while expanding the format to support new data types and workloads. The speaker described the new version as a major reimagining of the table format rather than an incremental step, with changes including a new metadata tree, more efficient commits, typed column statistics, relative file paths, and support for file and vector data types. While earlier versions left most of the metadata structure intact, V4 addresses problems that emerge at large scale and adds support for new use cases. Weeks told the audience in San Francisco:.

V4 is a major reimagining of a table format. We didn't get everything right in V3 and prior, so now we're taking the opportunity to fix some of the biggest things that are challenges as we scale up to even larger data sets and we bring on latest use cases.

Apache Iceberg is an open table format for managing large analytical datasets across different data processing engines. Originally developed at Netflix in 2017, it was open-sourced in 2018 and became an Apache top-level project in 2020. The main alternatives among open table formats are Delta Lake, created by Databricks and now a Linux Foundation project, Apache Hudi, originally developed at Uber, and Apache Paimon, which grew out of the Flink community and gained adoption for streaming-oriented workloads. However, interoperability tools are increasingly blurring the lines between them.

It has been revealed that in his talk, Weeks covered three areas of the proposed Iceberg V4 changes: metadata and scalability, including the Adaptive Metadata Tree, single-file commits, improved column statistics, relative paths, and column-level updates; latest table features, such as expression-based default values and constraints; and new data types, particularly file and vector types, which support additional workloads such as AI and search. Regarding faster commits, Weeks explained:.

It has been revealed that this gets us into use cases where we can stream data much faster. We can do commits at the 2nd level or subsecond level, where right now we largely recommend that you don't do commits under 2 minutes.

In a recent development, in V3, adding a data file requires at least four I/O operations, including manifest creation and rewriting. V4 simplifies this process by allowing the metadata tree's root to point directly to data files, reducing the operation to a single metadata write. According to Weeks, this could enable commits every second or even at subsecond intervals, compared with the current recommendation of at least two minutes between commits. Iceberg V3, introduced in 2024, added deletion vectors, row lineage, new data types, encryption, and default values.

Industry observers note that V4 replaces V3's binary column statistics with structured, typed statistics, improving projection and schema evolution. Furthermore, V4 introduces expression-based default values, check, unique, and primary key constraints, and statistics-only fields that support partitioning, sorting, and filtering without storing additional data. It will also track constraint validation status, allowing engines to determine when further checks are needed.

In August, Weeks started an initial V4 scope discussion on the Apache Iceberg developer mailing list, with Steven Wu suggesting adding monotonic snapshot and row-level update timestamps, while Manu Zhang discussed efficient column updates and the removal of equality deletes.

During the Q&A, Weeks explicitly confirmed that V4 metadata will not be backward compatible with older readers. Existing V3 metadata can remain in place during an upgrade, but older readers cannot consume the latest representation.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Notable features in this release include the introduction of the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command to optimize tables without disruption to ongoing operations, better control over blueprint stability and query performance with the new pg_plan_advice extension, and a number of performance improvements.

In September, LWN covered the removal of several features initially slated for this release. See the release notes for a full list of latest features and changes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Sources indicate that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

Sources indicate that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

According to recent reports, overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All newly introduced data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

In a recent development, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

In a recent development, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the upcoming release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Sources indicate that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

It has been revealed that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Recent findings suggest that proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been confirmed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team confirmed the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Industry observers note that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.
