💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • In a recent development, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

In a recent development, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post demonstrates you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

In a recent development, reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

According to recent reports, if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Recent findings suggest that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Industry observers note that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

According to recent reports, the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Industry observers note that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

Industry observers note that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

It has been revealed that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

In a recent development, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Sources indicate that the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

Recent findings suggest that A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Sources indicate that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

In a recent development, both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Recent findings suggest that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

In a recent development, * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

Sources indicate that the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Industry observers note that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

In a recent development, training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

According to recent reports, reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can enhancement the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Patch: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

According to recent reports, optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Recent findings suggest that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one enhancement behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Sources indicate that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Recent findings suggest that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Industry observers note that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Sources indicate that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Industry observers note that our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Sources indicate that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Sources indicate that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

It has been revealed that one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Sources indicate that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise.

Jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

Jayesh Bhayani is Senior Engineering Director at Tesco, playing a central role in leading technology strategy and shaping business direction. His work focuses on creating strategic clarity, architectural direction, and organizational alignment needed for the business to compete at pace in an increasingly disruptive retail environment, driving enterprise scale and agentic commerce readiness.

According to recent reports, software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Jayesh Bhayani: I'm going to spend some time in sharing our learnings of transformation at scale at Tesco. That's why modernizing technology at Tesco. How it has changed the culture, not just within the organization, along with systems, but enabled the growth for the company. From that perspective, after 10 years being at Tesco, I thought it would be good to share the learnings we had from here and how we are looking at the future.

I was in California, in Silicon Valley, for about 25 years, when Tesco reached out to me, saying, would you like to work at Tesco? I had got no concept of Tesco, because I had never come to London before that. When I looked at the website, it was a pretty basic website. The outside-in perspective, when you look at the website of a large grocery chain, feels like there is no technology. This went on for a few months. After that, they convinced me to talk to a few people in the technology department. The state that this technology was, and what was needed for growth and the transformation that was needed at scale, was what motivated me and my wife. We were empty nesters already by that time. We decided, why not? Came here. Just around that time, Trump got elected. We felt even better.

First of all, some context into how large Tesco is. There are about 5,000 stores. Some of them are super. Some of them are medium. Some of them are small. They are across five different countries. We used to be in Asia as well, when I started 10 years back, in Thailand, Malaysia. We divested those businesses. We are still in five countries. We have 20 distribution centers. We have 25 million customers. That's almost one-third of the UK population. That's not small. We have 350,000 colleagues across our stores. Out of that, maybe around 15,000 in head office. Out of that, around 6,000 in technology. Again, it's big. It's big operations, large number of colleagues. We do around 50 million baskets. Not number of transactions, the baskets, which means the orders across our estate in our stores. We do 1.3 million online orders in a week. When COVID came, many companies talk about scale.

In a recent development, when COVID happened, when entire business shifted towards online, our challenge was to double the number of online slots that we can make available for our customers. By that time, for the e-commerce part, our platform was already live. When we doubled it, that's equivalent of putting almost three other competitor companies online in one month. Many companies stopped taking orders. Many companies stopped signing customers. We doubled it in a month. That again shows the scale. Fifty million cases through supply chain, huge. We are not even talking about number of miles the trucks travel and the logistics within the distribution center. We do 4.5 billion calls a day. We have 98% UK coverage when I talk about 25 million customers, but coverage-wise in terms of online business, that can cover the entire geography of UK. We cover almost 98%, which means you can have your home delivery of grocery done in 98% of the UK.

Industry observers note that tills, as we call it here in the UK, POS systems, as called in many other countries, almost 50,000. That's just POS devices. We are not talking about all other thousands and tens of thousands of handheld devices that run on the same platform. That's just the context, because that sets a very different tone for the kind of technology, how mission-critical technology becomes. Then driving transformation through that is quite challenging, because I worked at startups. I've worked at mid-size companies. I had my own startup. Being in California and not having a startup is a crime. I tried that, too. I worked at Yahoo for 10 years. I worked at large companies, worked at startups. Tesco is yet another scale. I wanted to reflect here, because it drives quite a lot of complexities in decision-making of what would you do with your transformation and technology choices.

It has been revealed that this goes beyond retail. Any industry that has got physical estate, digital, and real-time operations will face these complexities. That's where we learned about being both efficient and effective. Efficient is do things well, fast. Effective, do good things, which are more effective. A slight difference in nuances. You can be doing fast all the things, but if those are not the right things, you are chasing wrong goals. Do the right things and do things the right way, efficiency and effectiveness. I wanted to share here, this is not just about retail. This will apply to many of the industries who operate at that kind of scale and complexity.

Sources indicate that let's start as to why. Ten years back, why did we need transformation? It was quite a poor state within technology I'm talking. When they talked about a large grocery tech giant and I was thinking there is no technology inside, there was a lot of technology, but it was very siloed. Multiple technology stacks tied to historical business structures. When I'm talking siloed, this is not just, store had a POS system and e-commerce had something else. I'm talking multiple stacks within online or e-commerce business itself. Grocery, its entire stack. We had marketplace back then, completely different stack. One Microsoft, .NET, one Oracle. F&F, our clothing, Tesco wine. Customers across these, forget having single account, did not even have single login. Jayesh@groceryhomeshopping is different than Jayesh@marketplace, is different than Jayesh@f&f. We had no single customer view, no data platforms, no product management, nothing. It was that fragmented. There was no single identity, as I just explained.

No single source of truth for stock or pricing. From that perspective, when you have multiple monolithic systems running in private data centers, we were not in public cloud back then. It was not even private data cloud. It was just a bunch of machines. You would be lucky if you asked for a server and you get a server in two months. That was the state. Decades old POS system, 20 years old software running on our POS systems in the stores, completely batch oriented. You couldn't connect to them. The deployments were the engineers would go with the floppy disk and then will deploy the software in the stores. Third-party solutions, not just third-party solutions, they were heavily customized, because when you are at the scale of Tesco, you can demand saying, I need a slightly different thing in your software. Sounds good initially. Then you're locked in with a very customized version of vendor solution for multiple years.

In a recent development, we had software running from vendor solutions that were at least a decade old. You can't even upgrade them. Then heavily outsourced resources as well. These were where we had lots of consulting firms providing resources for us. Not a good culture, not good quality. You can imagine what the landscape was when we started 10 years back. At the scale of Tesco, that becomes quite complex to say, how do you find your journey through that?

Recent findings suggest that that got us the imperative for change, saying we definitely need omnichannel experience, because customer expectations were moving very fast. The old style of doing business was not working. Technology was not helping business. Business had all the motivation to change. Technology was stuck. We had hit the wall, literally. Global coherence across physical and digital estate, both. Rapid change cycles. Back then, as I mentioned, if you talked to a vendor and asked for a solution in our POS systems, it would be six months for minor changes. Regression on top of that, so three things would be broken. You do the testing, and they charge you for fixing the bugs again. It would be six to nine months before you could get anything out on our Tills or POS systems in stores. Forget e-commerce. Then along with that, of course, we needed higher reliability, higher capability. We needed omnichannel experience, higher security, everything.

It needed more capability and capacity, both. That led to us chasing from fragmented stacks to unified platforms that could serve all our channels across all our markets and develop a multi-tenant platform. That's what we developed. It was called only platform. Sometimes platform terms are confusing. I'm not talking just the tech platform. I'm talking about the retail platform that runs our business. Where are we now? All of our entire UK business and Republic of Ireland business runs on this platform, 100%. We are making inroads in our Central European businesses. In a recent development, this I describe in my own language. Let's now talk about the journey of transformation. Most of the enabling function, as we call it internally, which is back-office applications like people system, finance system, everything, they're not a core differentiator. The retail platform is a core differentiator, including the POS system that runs on every single Tills. You go to Tesco, that's our homegrown system. When you use your scan-as-you-shop device, some of you might be shopping in Tesco, you use those handheld devices, completely synced, runs on the same platform.

Recent findings suggest that every single device runs on our platform. Cameras runs on our platform. Everything runs on our platform. Those are the core differentiator. Where we buy, platform integration is a must. That's how we say. Platform and domain boundaries. Now, centralization versus decentralization. The reason why I mentioned this here is if you're going through this space, and now even more so, 10 years on it's a different world with the agentic workforce that's coming. You can't centralize things. Gone are the days of change control board, architectural board, queue up in front of those pedestals and get your design reviewed and get your code reviewed and everything. We had to decentralize that. That's where we had to come up with very clear domain boundaries, good set of standards. Freedom within the guardrail, that's how we call it. Freedom within the framework with those guardrails to say how are we going to do it, and then you can decentralize that.

It has been revealed that tech excellence. Tech excellence is not just tech debt. We call it tech excellence, because it's proactive as well. It is not just, do we have a few bugs that we need to do? Or, do we need to patch our operating systems? Of course, yes. How are you taking care that you're not going to face into those challenges on an ongoing basis? Back then, there was no concept of total loss recovery. How do you blueprint for total loss recovery? This is not DR. DR is basic. When you're talking about total loss recovery, it's a completely different ballgame. The kinds of capabilities you need for that, we start to put that into tech excellence. Because it's very easily assumed, even within technology, and I'm not talking outside technology. Of course, business teams don't have that level of understanding. Even within technology, anyone who is not in engineering will assume that this gets done by some engineers who had a good coffee on a good day on the side of their desk.

In a recent development, it doesn't happen that way. You have to dedicate time for that. You have to dedicate focus for that. That requires education. Outside engineering, that requires education. Outside technology, as well, at some point. Where now our business leaders talk about tech excellence saying, are you sure it's built right? It's needed. That's the cultural change we are talking about. That creates the framework for a much faster pace of delivery and clear ownership, as I said, with the clear domain boundaries, and strong and long-term resilience.

In a recent development, that strategic framework gave us, what are the core tenets of our platform? Only customer is not enough. Yes, we are driven by customer. That drives our business. If you only think about customers, that's not enough. For the size of Tesco, when you've got almost half a million people working for you, colleague experience is equally needed. All the systems that we run in our stores, the operational systems that we run for our business operations, everything needed to be transformed, not just the customer-facing applications. Partners, we had very poor rating from our suppliers back then. We had to establish the trust, but also build the systems to make sure that our suppliers, partners, people who give us potatoes and tomatoes to sell for grocery, I'm referring to those partners, not tech partners, we had to improve experience for that. Reuse across multiple different markets and business units.

Sources indicate that offline operations. When you are talking about thousands of edge devices working in your stores, one of the most critical requirements for us is a network can be flaky. Because if you get in the business of replacing network of your entire thing, you might be spending hundreds of millions. Grocery is a very low margin business, it's around 4%. Some are 3%, some are 4%, some are 4.5%. It's a very low margin business. Every penny that you spend counts, goes in your P&L. Cyber risk and compliance built-in into the platform. Super key. This is where we had to innovate across all three public clouds. We did create private cloud, not just a server sitting in our data centers, and edge platform as well. As I was just referring to low margin business, cost is a feature for us, not a constraint. We don't see cost as a constraint.

According to recent reports, it's a very different mindset. As part of one of our learnings, we'll go through the learnings, but since we are talking about that, when we jumped into public cloud, and this now will apply into agentic code development as well, and we are thinking through that. The value that gets created against the cost that you might be spending, you've got to be very careful about that. We were spending upwards of £50 million, £60 million on public cloud. I'm talking four, five years back. It was growing exponentially. If you don't control that, then you've got £50 billion business, which was back then, with 4% margin, you're talking about £2 billion. When you talk £100 million of just cloud cost, I'm not talking our salaries, I'm not talking about entire technology department, this is just cloud cost. You can imagine how much P&L you are impacting at that level. It's the responsibility of the technology department to say, how do you keep cost as a feature, not as a constraint?

According to recent reports, then we came up with good principles for our platform, which, as I noted, domain design was very important. Create composable services. Data pathways and data quality both matter. You need very clear data pathways as to how data would flow between the various different operating datasets to data lakes, but also data quality across each one of these steps. Security in a layered defense model, all the way from perimeter to built inside. We got tons of different layers of how do you think about security. Multi-tenancy by default, which is, you build the platform once. Even from the physical deployment perspective is the same deployment that works and enables multiple countries for us, multiple different businesses. Build product capabilities, not just solutions, not point solutions. Build products, build capabilities. Then abstractions, all of you will understand that. It's not just for hiding complexity but also when you got mobile applications running across thousands of microservices, running in the data center or in the cloud.

In a recent development, for example, add an item to your shopping cart has got at least 40 different microservices called. Get the identity token, get the product ID, get the customer UUID, get their personalization preferences, get the price, check all that, get the product description. After that, it goes in the basket. Now if you are not creating abstractions that's going all the way from someone's mobile phone all the way to your data center or public cloud, and adding an item if it takes 40 network round trips, you are extremely slow. Yes, it is of course for hiding complexity, but at this scale all that matters. That's what went into our principles because that created cohesion across, as I was saying, digital and physical estate without becoming bottleneck.

In a recent development, that was one of the lessons learned to say, while you are trying to do that, sometimes it's good to build more centralized capabilities first before you jump into that. It takes a little longer but saves you costly migration. From that perspective, any services that needs true elasticity and scalability we put it in public cloud. Public cloud is a dual-edged sword because when you start using PaaS, Platform as a Service, you get very tightly bound to that public cloud because many of them are very proprietary services. You will never get out of that. You lose your flexibility. As Tesco, at our scale, we like that flexibility. Whether it is when we buy the technologies for our use, deployed or in the cloud, anywhere, we care a lot about saying, does it give us flexibility or not? Because if you're not careful, the license fees keep on increasing exponentially.

Sources indicate that if you are locked in, it's a very well-known fact that you will be held hostage. If you don't use PaaS then it's just a compute environment. Why are you in public cloud in the first place? You see, it works both ways. What we try to use is all portable PaaS technologies within the public cloud, that gives us that freedom. It's not perfect. I will not claim that. That does give us an optionality when it's needed. Then, many of our large systems, we are talking about supply chain systems, distribution centers, technologies related to that, we tend to run that into our private cloud. It's almost 80-20, 80% of our presence is in private cloud, 20% is in public cloud. Cost-wise, exact flip of that, 80% of the cost is in public cloud, 20% of the cost is in private cloud. It costs almost 8 to 10 times more for an equivalent setup in public cloud.

Sources indicate that this is where as we are talking about agentic code development and everything, a developer could spend almost £500 a day without realizing or without clarity on what value is getting created. Again, if you step back historically this is where public cloud was almost 10 years back. Easy to jump in, hard to explain what value is getting created. The learnings here that we are talking while the technology will keep on evolving is pretty much where you can reapply.

In a recent development, then comes the edge part of it. As I was saying, when you are at the scale and you want omni-channel experience, how do I now create a platform that is going to power your edge as well? What we did was, the same platform services, the microservices that run in our cloud, they run in our scaled environment with the right abstractions in our edge devices as well. There is a real consistency of business logic. There is a real consistency from data perspective, because when the network is there it's constantly exchanging data. For whatever reason, if the network is not available, we are able to identify the customer. If you have a club card, we identify your loyalty. We fail in favor of our customer. Let's say you did disable your club card literally last minute and network is chopped off and you are in the store, yes of course, that's a real-time requirement, but we fail in favor of our customers.

We take the payment, not cash, credit card as well. Very lately we have enabled contactless payment as well. That's a huge set of capabilities. It's pretty much, you don't realize the store is running offline. The pricing on the shelf edge, that has to be considered. Now as many companies are talking about electronic shelf edge labels, that's part of our consideration in the platform, saying, what happens when the network is not running. How would you upgrade prices on the shelf edge labels? All this gets very taken for granted. Even I wasn't aware as to what's the level of complexity when you are in a retail business with hundreds of thousands of such devices running across thousands of stores. One part which we made sure was, it's the same team which is responsible for edge platform as well as our retail platform in the cloud. That made sure that consistency was there, that ownership was there.

In fact, when we were migrating from legacy stack and we were transforming, we made sure it's the same team that owned the legacy platform as well. You cannot compartmentalize and outsource the problem even within the technology department, saying, A team is building newly introduced services and A team will take care of the old services. Never works. You lose motivation very promptly.

This is where we were talking about workload placement. We touched upon this a little bit before, which is, a single team owns that thing. We do use portable PaaS technologies when we are using the public cloud. In public cloud, we generally favor the systems that need scale and they are closer to the customer from that perspective. We, for the private environment in data centers, enabled the cloud as well so that for the developers it's the same experience when you are in the private cloud. We centralized a lot of our shared services. What initially started as, and this is probably a misconception, me being in technology, I'm 35 years in technology, that engineers love doing all these things. Setting up your Cassandra's, setting up your Kafka's, figuring out all the protocols. Yes, all that is true in the beginning part of the transformation. As we started putting more and more production workloads, because early on as part of our talent transformation we decided there is no separate QA team, there is no separate support team.

Sources indicate that of course, first-line support is different, but then pretty soon the call does come to our engineers so they are fully responsible for support of production environment. What started as a good challenge, as a good hobby, learning new technologies, pretty soon became very onerous. When I talk about creating shared services, so I own the retail platform, I own the tech platform, we'll talk about tech platform at Tesco, and I own the applications as well. It's not as much fun for engineers today to say, I'm going to deploy my own Cassandra, I will do the partitioning, and I will do all these things. It gets very onerous at some point. We invested a lot in shared services to say, how do you now not worry about all these things?

It has been revealed that the sequence is very important. When we started 10 years back, and we are talking about a company which is 100-plus years old, when we were talking about product development, the misconception in the business teams was, prepared meals in a box is called product. That was the journey when we started. When we started talking about platforms, we had to choose our sequence in the right way. You can never do Big Bang. You cannot ask a 50 billion business to stop and pause and say, we will come back in two years or one year or three years and we'll change everything. Even within that staggered approach, that you see from 2016, this is the real chart. In fact, we stopped counting at 2024, and we had only put significant items here. We had to pick our sequence. Initially it was very far and few in between. We had to develop and create that trust in technology from the business side to say, how are we going to figure this journey out.

There was a lot of distrust when we started. You have to find the right demand, where the business demand, the customer demand is there, and find the right opportunities to do transformation in small steps early on, and then it gets bigger and bigger. Now we get more demand from the business with more trust, less questions. You say, how can we do it right?

Industry observers note that we have been using AI for a very long time at Tesco. That's nothing latest for us. For example, start with all those business units I was saying, supply chain. One of the biggest challenges is forecasting how much customers would buy. If you go wrong in that one, it either leads to loss in millions or very poor customer experience. For example, if you forecast that you will sell 100kgs of tomatoes. It's in tons generally. I'm just taking an easy number. Except if you go wrong, either your shelves will be empty because customers are buying more and you need more than 100kg, or you will end up buying too much and it goes to waste. That's a tiny example, but that whole forecasting is dependent upon what's the lead time to getting the products.

In a recent development, like tomatoes can be supplied four times in a day in our distribution center. Something like jeans might be six months in advance. Then the shelf life could be very different. Tomatoes will get rotten in few days, non-perishable items will stay on the shelf for longer time, so the combination of that. That's the supply chain side. Distribution, how are you going to lay out all that stock? What's the stock management? What's the truck routing algorithms? Because we are talking about hundreds and thousands of miles of trucks traveling every day. How are you going to optimize that? Good for environment, good for manufacturer, good for everyone. How do you fill the truck? This is just touching into the supply chain area. Likewise, when you talk about ranging, you talk about customer experience in personalization, you talk about pricing, everything is AI driven. How are we thinking about agentic commerce?

It has been revealed that because that changes the paradigm completely. What I said is agentic commerce is a business decision. Because if you don't participate in agentic commerce, you can be marginalized. If you go there, you can still be marginalized because you're losing the first touch, customer experience. Because now you outsource that experience to someone else. Hence, it's a business decision. It's not just a technology decision. Getting ready requires complete shift. How would you be ready for agentic commerce? We'll look at the architecture as to how you will prepare for that kind of integration. You will need the same kind of identity consent and policy frameworks as to how much you can allow the agents to operate on your website or through your APIs. Then multiple protocol interfaces are emerging, UCPs, ACPs. The platform completely evolves from a system of record, that's how it used to be, to a system of delegation. Because now those agents are working with your data, with your services, making decisions for the customer. It's a complete delegation.

Recent findings suggest that that's the harness, how we are thinking. We are still going to use the platform because the core capabilities are still within our retail platform. If you look at the bottom left, customers, the bottom part is the existing path, existing online channels or stores from that perspective, existing application gateway, existing experience APIs going into our platform, retail platform. When you're talking about the agents on the top, you'll need now the gateways for the agents. How would you allow them? How much would you allow them? Which one would you allow them? The commerce protocol, ACP and UCP, now there are severe regulations in the UK for making payments, not allowed for agents to make payments on behalf of customers. Again, there are differences between the countries and regions to say what is allowed, what is not allowed. Many of these technologies, and I'm talking about both UCP, ACP, we are in direct conversation, are not ready for production scale yet.

In a recent development, as much as there is marketing, they are not ready. For Tesco scale, again you need very different readiness. We are not even talking about risk and compliance and anything here. I'm just talking pure technology risk here. Then you will have your own sub-agents that might be running, which might be talking to these agents and hence agent-to-agent protocol. You will need MCP for discovery of many of these services, discovery of data. Many of our application experience APIs were built for the applications that we built, like add item to basket, for example. You might need those plus some more for the agentic experience, but going back into the same retail platform. That's how we are looking into the future and thinking how we are going to do that.

What could have been better is, build central tech platform early. As I remarked, we jumped in early into the public cloud and then we realized that everyone had their own version of CI/CD platforms and observability and everything. Now when I was talking to my own teams, say, we got best CI/CD pipelines, and every team was saying that. I don't need 50 CI/CD pipelines, I need one CI/CD pipeline. Portfolio management, we introduced that a bit late, but that where the products are matured when you're talking about 6,000 people in technology and hundreds of products, you need a very good management of where you are going to put your investment, where the value is. The portfolio management becomes very important. We use product maturity model for that now to say, our product is mature or not mature, and it can go left and right in the maturity curve.

In a recent development, location strategy. Most companies, they assume that engineering can be even in-sourced where they are your own teams. They can be in various different locations, but if you're not careful, product management sits somewhere else, engineering sits somewhere else, program sits somewhere else. Try to create self-sufficient teams. I touched on three parts of those transformation, a little bit of each one of them to say what's important. There are many more in that one. The biggest point was the more you step back and think about it, you will avoid costly re-implementation and migration. That's huge. It spends a lot of time and spend of cost.

Industry observers note that final two slides on what are some of the tips if you are following the transformation at scale. Three pillars, we talked about that. Just system transformation is not enough. Change business processes when required, because they are just organically developed like your technology systems as well. Question that to say, is that really different? Why should four different countries have different operational processes? Simplify operation. Build core capabilities, we just talked about that. Because now we have the tech platform which supports this retail platform for those same CI/CDs, the observabilities, everything, but we could have started that early. Start that early. Throughput is a long game. Today also we get a lot of pressures, and can we go live in two months? Can we go live in two weeks? Can we go live in three weeks? We can do that if the platform capabilities are there. Total throughput is much higher today, but the same thing could have taken us six months long back when we had to develop those capabilities.

Sources indicate that if we didn't do that, now we can do 10 such things and we would never have done that because we would have just duplicated it. Evolve continuously. We used to be very horizontally laid. I ran entire engineering of Tesco, all the platforms, all this thing, but product management was separate. Now that platforms are matured, we are going more vertical. I still run the platforms because that we cannot divide. The core platform is still there, but the application domain wise now we are creating more partnership between business and people like me within technology. Evolution is necessary. E-commerce is not just enough. Avoid tech for tech. Communicate value early. It's very hard to understand outside technology for sure. What are you all doing, is the frequent question we get. How come you are so many people? What's going on? It has gone less and less now. Even within technology, it's hard to explain what value we have created for the business.

We talked about the cost, IP and vendor lock-in. We are very careful when we are talking about agentic code development. We are very careful as to what kind of IP leakage could happen. Vendor lock-in, we talked about it. Even when we use many of the SaaS solutions, we ask for those protections from data sharing perspective, from IP perspective, so that we keep that edge of differentiation for Tesco. Then last one is technology will keep evolving, but if you have set the right culture, I mean there was blockchain there, public cloud before that, MapReduce systems, now agentic part. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TorchNeuron provides a latest native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • Industry observers note that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a latest native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

Industry observers note that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Sources indicate that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

It has been revealed that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

In a recent development, text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

According to recent reports, now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Recent findings suggest that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

It has been revealed that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

It has been revealed that the command below debuts training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

It has been revealed that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

In a recent development, more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

According to recent reports, make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Sources indicate that hi, which models are supported with this? is mobernbert and t5gemma2 on the list?

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support.

#138117. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1343 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Sources indicate that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and newly introduced Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Sources indicate that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each latest token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

In a recent development, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The latest Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Sources indicate that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

In a recent development, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them latest paths through Metal:.

Industry observers note that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Sources indicate that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

In a recent development, scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Sources indicate that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

According to recent reports, pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hatedabamboo

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Terraform initiative passes and highlights all green and all the necessary resource changes.
  • Sources indicate that the problem with the difference between proposal and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure.
  • There are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Terraform initiative passes and highlights all green and all the necessary resource changes. You trigger apply and... the job fails with some obscure error that a resource can't be changed. You open another pull request and try again. And perhaps you encounter an error again. Sounds familiar? I bet it does. I encountered issues like this so many times I'm afraid to count. But recently AWS released a latest tool called Emulator that emulates actual AWS API endpoints. And it should be great for tasks just like that!

Sources indicate that the problem with the difference between proposal and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure. It's a safe assumption based on the static declarations we put into it – the order of application, the necessary parameters, the proper configuration values. These mock calls can't know for a fact that you already have a resource in AWS called "my-bucket-asdasdasd" or that you're trying to upgrade a PostgreSQL RDS instance from version 14 to version 18 without an explicit "apply immediately" flag. One may argue that one can always try to apply changes locally, but this kinda undermines the whole automation workflow. So what is the answer?

There are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture. It may be similar, but it won't be authentic, and sometimes this small difference may cause a lot of problems. After all, what can be the closest to an AWS API, if not the same AWS API, but ephemeral?

In a recent development, the benefit of the AWS Emulator is that it's a self-contained binary (or Docker container) that can be utilized locally or in a CI workflow. This means the usual "Plan > Apply" terraform workflow changes to "Plan > Apply against mock AWS infrastructure to test the plan > Apply on actual AWS Infrastructure". This means slightly longer jobs, but if you're like me and apply jobs run on commits to the main branch after a PR, this saves you the hassle of creating a new branch just to fix the issue.

Let's start with a local setup and see how we can utilize AWS Emulator with the actual Terraform code. All code is available in my example GitHub repository.

First up, installation. You can either install aws-emulator via package manager, or build it with Docker. I'll use Docker to keep my system clear of yet another package:.

And it's up and running! In the example above I set the container to live without limits (official AWS documentation proposes to set memory and swap limits: --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g, but for local that's fine). I also disabled authorization (flag -a off) to simplify things a bit.

To be sure aws-emulator is up and running, let's query the admin endpoint:.

Okay, fake AWS is live, let's deploy some infrastructure!

Sources indicate that I created an example AWS stack for Terraform and will use it in this article. First, let's configure Terraform to act against aws-emulator and not real AWS APIs. providers.tf will look like this:.

The difference between actual live infrastructure and a fake one is that we set up a bunch of flags to allow insecure connections (perhaps turning authentication off wasn't actually simpler?) and we set up an endpoint for each service we use in the setup to an emulator endpoint, which lives in the local Docker container:.

According to recent reports, the rest of the configuration is as usual: resources, variables, modules (if any). Just what your project has.

In a recent development, let's proceed and test our setup. (I'll omit full terraform output otherwise this article would be 3 kilometers long).

Strategy works! That's good to see, but not what we're here for. Still, a good sign. Now for the real test.

Sadly, the running aws-emulator container doesn't show in its logs which API requests it receives and what's happening under the hood, but I guess the tool is good enough as it is.

When you're done, stop the container:.

A container started with --rm removes itself after stopping, so no additional cleanup is needed. And as for the emulator -- it stores its state in memory, so each container restart drops all record of previous actions and any stale state.

Now for the real test: can we wrap the desired logic inside a CI pipeline? Let's think.

For successful invocation in the pipeline we will need almost everything the same, but we will be limited by time (the faster -- the better, and overall reasonable timeouts) and resources.

It has been revealed that the workflow with terraform apply against aws-emulator is shown down below. For it I decided to try out package manager installation (builders are ephemeral anyway) and proper authentication. Full workflow with actual successful runs can be found in the example GitHub repository.

This is a crude excerpt of the actual glorious workflow file that outlines the most important steps: emulator installation, terraform setup, plan and apply. On the example terraform architecture the whole pipeline took 1m25s, which is okay in my opinion, but there is room for improvement: sprinkle some caching on top, leave validation, format check for local hooks, etc.

Industry observers note that it's always nice when code someone wrote on the internet works from the start after you copy-paste it onto your machine. That's why I always run the described processes myself -- building, testing, fixing, retrying -- before publishing an article. But showing only the positive scenarios creates a false sense of trust in the tool.

Let's break something on purpose.

According to recent reports, in the example codebase I added a variable that, when enabled, makes the stack try to deploy a resource with an erroneous declaration. It will pass the plan job, but fail on apply.

According to recent reports, setting this variable to true at runtime will break our stack. Let's see:.

And there we have it. The exact problem that arises only against actual API calls and not during a initiative job.

For scenarios exactly like this, the emulator is priceless.

AWS Emulator is AWESOME. I'm rarely that excited about fresh tools lately (mostly because almost all of them are near/about AI), but this one is just so good and scratches that exact itch I felt for so long.

For starters, it can't effectively emulate IAM policies and permission checks. This is a bummer, because permission validation is such a crucial step for production-ready security. Here's hoping that the tool will evolve further and it will be included in future updates.

According to recent reports, second, as a tool still a work-in-progress[1], its capabilities are quite limited. Even while writing the article I encountered several cases of 501 NotImplemented. It complicates things a bit if your infrastructure setup is huge and has a lot of quirks and weird configurations and super newly introduced services. Still, AWS releases new versions quite often, and they're quite open about Emulator limitations, which is nice.

And last, but not least, is telemetry. AWS is explicit that it gathers telemetry and what this telemetry includes. This is honest behaviour and I like that approach. They even allow you to disable the telemetry, which further increases my trust in this tool. I understand the rationale behind this functionality (the tool is actively developed, they need the data to understand usage patterns and what goes wrong), but in the age of constant surveillance from Big Tech at every corner it still raises a slight concern. But then again, for the ultra-paranoid folks the code is open source and can be rebuilt with telemetry torn out of it.

As of the moment of writing this article, AWS Emulator has been live for 1 day. ↩︎.
