💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

In a recent development, A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

Industry observers note that at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS states nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space demonstrates comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Recent findings suggest that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

AI Governance in 2027: Accountability Moves Into the Workflow

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them.
  • That gap will become harder to defend in 2027.
  • The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them. They ask for a review. Somewhere inside the organization, a policy names an accountable executive—but the support team cannot find anyone authorized to change the result. Governance exists on paper. The person is still stuck.

That gap will become harder to defend in 2027. As AI moves into ordinary operations, accountability will have to become something an organization can exercise while a disputed decision is still affecting someone's life.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations. My expectation for 2027 is that buyers will ask for evidence of these practices inside operating workflows. The following predictions concern organizational accountability, rather than a promise that a particular checklist can make every AI system fair.

Industry observers note that the most revealing name on an AI governance chart is the person who can say stop. In 2027, more organizations will describe roles with genuine authority to suspend or change a deployment. That changes the meaning of ownership: responsibility becomes a decision right, with consequences for a project somebody else may be eager to keep running.

In a recent development, responsibility without authority creates a ceremonial owner. A governance lead can maintain an inventory while a product team changes the model, a supplier changes the service, and an operations team changes the decision threshold. No single person necessarily controls the consequences of the resulting system.

In a recent development, the Govern function in the NIST framework connects roles and organizational risk management. The NIST Playbook offers practical actions that organizations can adapt. These are voluntary resources, not evidence that adopters already execute them well.

Industry observers note that the development I expect is a more concrete chain of authority: who can accept a use case, who can narrow its scope, and who can stop it when the evidence changes. Different decisions can belong to different roles. What matters is that the authority survives ordinary commercial pressure and is exercised against a documented standard. A well-written responsibility chart that nobody uses would not demonstrate the predicted change.

In a recent development, look for published suspension criteria, records of actual governance decisions, and escalation paths beyond the product's revenue owner. A policy naming an accountable executive without explaining what that executive can change would provide weaker evidence than an operational case study.

Assign decision rights before expanding a deployment. Buyers should ask who can authorize exceptions and whether the risk function can halt a workflow without the supplier's consent. Founders can shorten enterprise reviews by making these responsibilities visible in the product and service agreement.

Industry observers note that an explanation can tell someone why a decision happened and still leave them powerless to correct it. I expect enterprise products to make challenges more practical in 2027, preserving the original evidence and recording what the reviewer decides. The test of the feature will be what happens after the person claims the system has missed something important.

An explanation and an appeal solve different problems. An explanation tells a person what supposedly happened. An appeal gives them a route to change an outcome that may be wrong, incomplete or inappropriate for their circumstances. A generic support form can satisfy neither need if the reviewer cannot reconstruct the original decision.

The OECD guidance treats due diligence as a continuing process involving impacts and responses. That makes remediation a useful commercial design question as well as an ethical one. My forecast is that some vendors will turn it into a repeatable workflow rather than leave each customer to improvise.

In a recent development, the difficult part will be the reviewer's independence and access to context. Re-running the same model with slightly different wording is not a meaningful challenge process. Nor should preserving evidence require indiscriminate retention of sensitive personal information. The system needs enough decision context to support correction while honoring appropriate retention and access limits.

Look for the ability to submit missing facts, reach a qualified human reviewer, and receive a recorded disposition. Reversal rates and time to correction will be more revealing than the existence of an appeal button. Unanswered queues would weaken the forecast's practical significance.

According to recent reports, budget for the people who handle contested decisions. A supplier's automation savings should be assessed alongside review workload and correction costs. Product teams should design evidence capture and access permissions with the appeal process, because reconstructing decisions afterward can be expensive or impossible.

According to recent reports, an internal drafting assistant can become a customer-screening tool through a series of apparently small product decisions. The launch approval may still be on file while the use case has changed underneath it. In 2027, more governance programs will revisit material changes in models, data and affected populations, treating approval as a continuing responsibility.

A system approved for drafting internal correspondence can become consequential when its output starts determining which customers receive an offer. The model may be unchanged; its social role has changed. Conversely, a supplier update can alter behavior while the customer-facing workflow looks identical.

ISO/IEC 42001 addresses organizational AI management, and ISO's discussion of 42001 and impact assessment connects management practices with evaluating effects. Neither makes a management-system certificate a guarantee that every output is accurate or every deployment is acceptable.

In a recent development, the practical challenge is proportionality. Repeating a full assessment for a spelling correction would overwhelm the process; ignoring a new affected population would undermine it. Organizations will need a defensible account of which changes alter the risk and which do not.

Look for specific reassessment triggers and examples where a deployment's conditions were narrowed after review. Version logs alone will be insufficient. Evidence that organizations compare real effects before and after a material change would strengthen this prediction considerably.

Include change notification and evaluation rights in supplier contracts. Internally, connect the model inventory to the systems that manage deployment changes. The objective is to identify changes that matter early enough to act, without turning every routine maintenance event into a board-level decision.

A certificate can become more reassuring than the evidence warrants. The harder commercial conversation is what it actually covers. In 2027, assurance and procurement documents will become clearer about the difference between an organization's management practices and the behavior of a particular deployment. That precision will make assurance more useful, even when it makes the sales claim less sweeping.

The more popular a governance label becomes, the more tempting it is to treat that label as a universal seal of safety. Yet different assurance exercises answer different questions. An audit of management processes cannot prove that a model behaves reliably for a population the evaluator never tested.

It has been revealed that ISO/IEC 42006 sets requirements for bodies auditing and certifying AI management systems. It is relevant to the quality of certification itself. It does not turn ISO/IEC 42001 into a product-performance benchmark. This distinction will become more commercially notable as suppliers use assurance credentials in sales processes.

According to recent reports, my confidence is lower here because incentives can favor broad reassurance over careful qualification. Still, sophisticated buyers have a reason to demand both organizational assurance and use-case evidence: they bear the consequences if a certified supplier's product fails in their workflow. Good assurance should make the remaining questions clearer, rather than imply that there are none.

Recent findings suggest that look for an explicit statement of the certified entity, scope, exclusions and validity period, alongside separate application testing. Claims that a certificate proves an AI system is unbiased or universally compliant would run against the direction predicted here.

According to recent reports, use certification to inform diligence, then evaluate the actual deployment. Suppliers should prepare a clear explanation of what their assurance covers. Buyers should ask which unresolved risks remain their responsibility and what evidence would justify accepting them.

Industry observers note that accountability becomes visible when the organization has a reason to resist it: an attractive launch, an expensive correction, a profitable use case that needs narrowing. The strongest governance stories in 2027 will show how those decisions were made—and whether the people affected had a meaningful way to be heard.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

Industry observers note that for example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

Sources indicate that using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

TLX introduces a fresh Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

Industry observers note that taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

Meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:.

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:.

Sources indicate that making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta intends to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with torch.compile.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • LFM2 indicated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

LFM2 indicated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

The payoff indicates at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

In a recent development, every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two newly introduced in-house encoders:.

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Recent findings suggest that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

It has been revealed that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a latest in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Industry observers note that reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

Sources indicate that LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

According to recent reports, we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Lean and Mathlib communities certified on November 21, 2026 that Levent Alpöge’s 17-million-line Lean library correctly states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis, following a day of compilation, statement-matching, and proof-kernel checks. Their joint statement was endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

Industry observers note that the certification follows Alpöge’s announcement on November 20, 2026, in which he mentioned he discovered and formalized the proof while working with Claude. The release contained only the Lean formalization; Alpöge viewed a conventional write-up at this stage as a huge, unreadable document and planned to understand, simplify, and explain the mathematics properly.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib, the community’s library of formalized mathematics. The statement being proved was already part of Mathlib and had been vetted by experts in Lean and number theory, addressing the requirement that the formal statement express the intended hypothesis. Dozens of people reported compiling the library without errors or build failures and reproducing the same raw proof export.

To check the theorem’s identity, a community-added challenge file isolated the Riemann Hypothesis statement and imported only Mathlib. Comparator and con-leche’s comparison mode independently confirmed that Alpöge’s theorem matched that statement exactly. The raw proof export was checked with Lean’s official kernel, con-leche, con-ron, and additional third-party checkers written in different programming languages.

Those checks ran on an inert export, beyond the reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean sources. Con-leche and con-ron also have formal proofs, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, addressing concerns that a flaw in Lean’s logic could be exploited.

Industry observers note that andrew Sutherland’s MIT verification record, last updated at 12:55 UTC on November 21, 2026, reports that all 175,187 modules compiled with zero errors using Lean and Mathlib version 4.33.1; his checks were run with Claude Code. An axiom audit found that the five headline theorems depended only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, with no axioms declared outside Lean core. Nanoda, an independent Rust kernel, and con-leche each accepted the full exported proof, lean4lean accepted every compiled module, and con-leche’s comparison mode matched every challenge statement.

Sources indicate that at that page’s cutoff, the Lean default and paranoid kernel checks on the export and the full lake comparator run remained in progress. Older bundled con-leche and con-ron binaries exited without a verdict because they did not support one reflexive inductive type, not because they rejected the proof. Sutherland also disclosed that the build ran on unsandboxed cloud machines and that its export hash had not been compared with one from a sandboxed lake build; a passing result still relies on the kernels used and on Mathlib’s definitions representing their intended mathematics.

The central theorem uses Mathlib’s formal definition: every zero of the Riemann zeta function other than the trivial zeros at negative even integers must have real part one-half. The separate condition s ≠ 1 appears because Mathlib assigns the zeta function a conventional value at its pole. The submission also verifies Generalized Riemann Hypothesis statements for Dirichlet L-functions across all moduli and characters; Sutherland expressly excludes Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions, and general automorphic L-functions from the checked scope.

According to recent reports, alpöge’s account assigns Claude a role in discovery as well as formalization: he guided the work from a toy setting into an analogous target situation before Claude outpaced him near the finish. In one example, Claude suggested that a von Mangoldt sum of length X should use a chain of theta lifts of length X, a technical choice Alpöge highlights in his explanation of the argument.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge describes the current argument as extremely long, expects substantial simplification, and is still working to understand and explain it. His account describes human guidance and Claude’s technical contributions, with both formalizing the arguments without extra assumptions. The certification concerns the formal artifact; that account supplies the basis for describing Claude’s role, rather than demonstrating an autonomous solution.

The certification resolves the formal-checking question without resolving the explanatory one. Whether the proof’s newly introduced ideas can be simplified and absorbed by mathematicians remains the central open question around the verified Lean library.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the Chinese government is keeping tabs on ethnic Chinese people abroad via an AI-powered Major Data mining program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Sources indicate that the CCP built a Substantial Data system to scrape reams of information and learn about individuals abroad, to potentially target and exploit them. Think Alice Huang Lite.

It has been revealed that the Chinese government is keeping tabs on ethnic Chinese people abroad via an AI-powered Major Data mining program. In some cases, the program is helping the government design influence operations targeting high-ranking individuals in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

Since the AI boom began, world leaders have been feeling out how to exploit it to cement their power. While Washington's emphasis has been on shorter-term AI ventures — tracking immigrants and political protestors, identifying social services to cut, etc. — the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has been building something more durable: a data center that facilitates gargantuan Web scraping from social media and other public sources, feeds the results into machine learning algorithms, and outputs actionable intelligence for the apparatchiks in Beijing.

Industry observers note that that's according to documents leaked to China watchdog NetAskari. In a report shared with Dark Reading and Sky News UK ahead of publication, NetAskari detailed a program that balances straightforward government PR with unsavory surveillance. Sometimes the data gathering has been designed around Cambridge Analytica-style targeted propaganda campaigns. In more nefarious cases, it has been used to identify individuals in political and economic spheres of interest who might one day make good spies or unwitting assets in spy campaigns.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge.

"A foreign nation with rather undemocratic tendencies is running an extensive, AI-charged analysis and information-scraping operation to find ways to influence other nations' internal social, economic, and political landscapes," a NetAskari analyst explains in an interview with Dark Reading over Signal. "That this system is particularly aiming at the Chinese diaspora, to see if [foreign citizens] can be used to further these ambitions, even if they might not be aware of it, is rather shocking.".

On Nov. 8, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang — one of the few most important people in the most important industry in the world — emailed his staff, admitting to an affair with a newly outed spy. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) agent, Alice Huang, redirected Nvidia semiconductors to China, where they're banned, and translated intelligence from the CEO to the CCP.

While the MSS ran Huang, the United Front Work Department (UFWD) took its own, less dramatic approach to the challenge of breaching Taiwan's semiconductor industry.

According to recent reports, the UFWD's main game is influence operations, at home and abroad, according to NetAskari. Its mission includes gauging and shaping media narratives about China abroad, engaging Chinese diaspora communities — to their benefit or detriment, depending on the situation — and, in certain cases, attempting to gain influence over powerful or otherwise useful individuals and organizations in China and abroad.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products.

In this instance, the UFWD appears to have been scoping out ethnic Chinese individuals involved in the semiconductor industry. A leaked report titled "Profiles of Ethnic-Chinese Leading Talent in the Chip Field, Their Circle Characteristics, and Work Recommendations" identifies executives of the Taiwanese AI company Skymizer, high-performing students at a top Taiwanese research university, and an AI research center director at Microsoft, among others, as individuals of note. It then details strategies for getting closer to these VIPs, like "leverage non-official organizations — hometown associations, alumni associations, professional societies — for relationship-building and cooperation.".

The system used to generate this report is called the "Overseas Chinese Affairs Massive Data Platform.".

The platform's brain is a 500-square-meter Big Data laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou, built to comfortably house rows of server racks and at least 100 employees.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks.

Basically, it's built to ingest massive amounts of online information about overseas Chinese communities, identify people, relationships, and public sentiments, and convert it all into actionable reports for CCP leadership, according to NetAskari.

Sources indicate that social media provides much of the content. The platform scrapes liberally from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and X, plus Chinese platforms like Weibo and WeChat. As a rule, the actual scrapers are run on machines located in foreign countries. As with Chinese hacking campaigns more broadly, the machines doing the crimes are also shielded behind rotating proxy networks. The goal of this obfuscation, one leaked document explains, is to “ensure the security of data collection and prevent the collection system from being traced and discovered" by targeted platforms.

The data then makes its way to China for processing. Foreign languages are translated into Chinese, keywords are extracted, and meaningful links are drawn. UFWD then cross-references these data with preexisting records of notable people identified as being involved in the media, sciences, politics, etc., as well as blacklisted and "two-faced people." These two sources feed a "business system" — the layer that seems to draw meaningful connections about public sentiments, the results of influence operations, and more.

Sometimes, the final reports outputted by this multitiered system simply concern public relations trends. Sometimes they've been used to identify ethnic Chinese individuals of note around the world — be they Taiwanese engineers, social media influencers, or something in between — and unearth strategies for how to utilize them to further the ends of the Chinese Communist Party.

Overall, the NetAskari analyst describes the Overseas Chinese Affairs Significant Data Platform as "a worldwide dragnet that uses open source intelligence (OSINT) and Big Data analysis to identify and find potential collaborators, partners, and affiliates that the UFWD can work with to further their goal [of] extending the Communist Party's influence abroad and creating a 'China-friendly' environment in other nations' political, economic, and social settings.".

Industry observers note that it's nothing the UFWD wasn't doing before, to be sure. Instead, the analyst adds, "What used to be done manually, at a much slower speed, is now supercharged via AI and modern technology.".

That, ultimately, is the rub. The leaked documents contain only outdated references, from 2021, about how machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms fit into this picture. It's unclear whether, and how, more modern large language models have been incorporated into — and potentially supercharged — the system. The better the AI gets, the more wide-ranging and granular the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform can become, with real consequences for people who may not know they are being targeted by a foreign nation.

In a recent development, "A surveillance state can't accept that its own citizens are escaping to other nations, outside the reach of Beijing's grasp. For the best part of the last 20 years, most people had the luxury to ignore this part of the Chinese state. Often practical and physical limitations restricted Chinese organiations to expand too promptly abroad or even get a foothold. But with remote methods like the ones we have seen applied in the Massive-Data center of Jinan University, these 'natural boundaries' don't apply anymore," the analyst laments.

"Pair it now with ever-growing globalization, China's stepping out onto the world stage, and crises of democracy in many Western nations, and it is not hard to see why such operations should concern even average citizens in the US or Europe," he notes. "Even if they have no personal ties to China.".

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

Sources indicate that he began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

Recent findings suggest that he holds degrees from Latest York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How Google Traced GKE API Timeouts to a Linux Kernel TCP Bug.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production.

In January, a customer running multiple GKE clusters with Private Service Connect (PSC) for private control-plane access experienced intermittent timeouts when pods attempted to reach the Kubernetes API server.

Packet captures revealed that the control plane was responding to new TCP connection requests with stale ACK packets belonging to previously closed connections. The root cause involved three separate bugs across different networking layers. Akash Thakur, senior technical solutions engineer at Google Cloud, describes how engineers across multiple Google teams identified three root causes and ultimately addressed them:.

Industry observers note that in a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

The investigation identified three interacting causes: packet reordering in PSC, Envoy's half-close behavior preventing TCP connections from being properly closed, and a Linux kernel bug that discarded certain reordered FIN packets.

It has been revealed that thakur describes a complex troubleshooting case involving I/O timeouts across Private Service Connect, virtual network interfaces, and the Linux TCP state machine, which ultimately revealed a kernel problem leaving sockets stuck indefinitely in the FIN_WAIT_2 state. Thakur explains:.

It has been revealed that most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

The glitch was addressed through three coordinated fixes over several weeks: Google first rolled back a Private Service Connect change to restore connectivity, then corrected the proxy protocol handling and added regression tests. Finally, a Linux kernel patch, authored by Eric Dumazet, formerly a software engineer at Google, fixed the underlying TCP issue. Rohan Karne, managing director at Google Cloud, comments:.

This is the unglamorous reality of mission-critical platform engineering—methodically ruling out the obvious suspects and digging into packet captures until you find the kernel root cause.

It has been revealed that thakur highlights how individually reasonable behaviors across networking, proxies and operating systems can combine into complex infrastructure failures. Packet captures at multiple network layers were essential to identifying the problem, while correlating network symptoms with infrastructure changes helped establish the connection between the three bugs. Guangba Yu, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, highlights:.

Recent findings suggest that for AIOps and chaos engineering, the transferable method is organizing simultaneous path observations, protocol state, and rollout events while distinguishing symptom recovery from state-machine correction. This anonymized case supplies no population failure rate and does not explain all API timeouts.

Justin Garrison, field CTO at Sidero, notes:.

According to recent reports, at first I was excited to read this article that leads to a kernel patch which are always fun. It turns out GKE just runs a kernel from 3 years ago (6.1) and the bug was already fixed upstream and they had to backport it.

The kernel fix was merged into Linux 6.9.7 and backported to the 6.6 and 6.1 LTS branches, reaching GKE customers in version 1.33.5 and later.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Recent findings suggest that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

It has been revealed that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's newly introduced speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

In a recent development, it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

It has been revealed that the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

According to recent reports, parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

According to recent reports, qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Industry observers note that qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Industry observers note that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Industry observers note that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who noted what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

In a recent development, the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

It has been revealed that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

According to recent reports, these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Sources indicate that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's latest is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Recent findings suggest that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Sources indicate that emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

According to recent reports, the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

It has been revealed that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

According to recent reports, raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Sources indicate that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

It has been revealed that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

According to recent reports, both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

According to recent reports, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

It has been revealed that try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Problems and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

  • Customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository.
  • Industry observers note that the coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts submitted to its serverless inference service. An AI coding agent had exposed the private-repository credential used in the download while the manufacturer was developing its public xorl GitHub repository.

Customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository. They involved requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026 and July 14, 2026.

Industry observers note that the coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development. Together AI’s automated scanning detected the exposure, and the company reverted the commit. During that exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored samples.

The sequence makes clear that detecting and reverting the commit did not prevent the credential from being used during the exposure window. The model names establish which requests were sampled, while the repository credential explains how the stored prompts became accessible.

After the download, the party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested whether they were valid. Five of the tested credentials were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment. The searches and validity tests show that the activity extended to possible reuse of secrets contained in prompts, creating a risk beyond disclosure of the prompt text itself.

Together AI worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement. The company said its review has not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident, that it has no reason to believe the data was leaked further, and that it understands the data has now been deleted.

Recent findings suggest that customer impact still depends on the content of the samples. The review is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed, and Together AI will contact affected customers directly as needed with findings relevant to them.

Industry observers note that together AI’s response includes scoped or short-lived credentials and keyless access where supported, credential checks on all pull requests, and updated development processes governing the use of AI coding agents. The company mentioned the credential measures are designed to reduce the potential impact of exposure, while the other changes add controls around pull requests and coding-agent development.

Zero data retention, abbreviated ZDR, is now the default setting for upcoming accounts. Together AI recommends that customers handling sensitive prompt data enable ZDR in their account settings and provides security@together.ai for questions about the incident or its potential impact on an organization.

The incident connects credential safety in AI-assisted development with the retention of customer prompts for testing. Together AI has documented controls for both, but the ongoing content review remains the decisive step in establishing what the exposure means for customers and which notifications are necessary.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super crucial for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

Industry observers note that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openRouter announced on November 22, 2026, that it had off-boarded three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention (ZDR), a setting under which prompts and responses are not stored. It also notified all potentially affected customers.

According to recent reports, the findings did not show a breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself, the tech giant said. The removals covered providers flagged by researchers and other endpoints withdrawn as a precaution. Its public list links notices from Novita, Phala and Together AI, but does not identify them as the three off-boarded providers; not all affected providers have published notices.

In research published on November 19, 2026, Dragos described submitting approximately two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary credentials to widely used AI services from July through November 2026, then monitoring subsequent activity. The tests produced evidence that data from at least three AI providers was exposed, that marketplace resellers viewed and retained customer prompts through standard logging, and that some providers appeared to disregard privacy settings or published policies.

In a recent development, the largest compromise involved a couple hundred seeded AWS keys sent during several short request windows in late October 2026. Some keys came from requests rejected before a model ran, which Dragos interpreted as evidence that copying occurred when requests first reached the provider rather than during model processing. The bait keys were subsequently used for tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

Sources indicate that the routing findings matter because every organization along a multi-hop path can see the complete prompt and response. Dragos traced about 2,000 inference routes: several hundred included an unidentified system, while in a handful, a company absent from the advertised path fetched the test image. Dragos also reported that one unnamed Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of prompts sent to its models between July and October 2026, including roughly two-thirds marked no-data-collection or ZDR.

Sources indicate that novita’s privacy notice remarked a routing configuration glitch broadened an API forwarding path intended for specific customers, sending some MiniMax requests to MiniMax’s official API rather than Novita-hosted infrastructure. Requests made directly through Novita or routed through OpenRouter between May 28, 2026, and November 11, 2026, may have had their contents accessed or retained by a third party. Novita suspended the affected models. The researcher observed accesses to test URLs and hostnames but no use of AWS test-key markers; automated content review may have been involved, an assessment Novita is checking with MiniMax.

In a recent development, phala’s preliminary incident report, published on November 10, 2026, advised users whose DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests were routed to Phala by OpenRouter from 00:00 UTC on October 21, 2026, to 05:35 UTC on November 8, 2026, to treat the contents as exposed and rotate included secrets. The attacker chained a legacy internet-facing service with management interfaces that trusted loopback access without independently authenticating callers. A similar access pattern gave the attacker control of an inference VM, making in-flight request data visible during processing.

Phala confirmed canary misuse only for requests sent on October 21–22, 2026, but kept the wider window because the tests sampled requests and could not reveal every possible data-access event. Containment was completed on November 8, 2026, and a full-platform audit found no evidence of compromise affecting other models or products. The investigation and verification of remediation remain active, with a full root-cause analysis planned.

Industry observers note that together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after an AI coding agent committed a credential for a private Hugging Face repository to the public xorl GitHub repository. Collected for routine software testing with authorization, the samples came from MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 requests, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026, and July 14, 2026. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, including five Dragos canary credentials.

Together noted it has not identified additional prompt leakage beyond the incident, but its review of affected prompt contents and determination of which customers require direct notification remain ongoing. Its changes include scoped or short-lived credentials, credential checks on all pull requests, ZDR by default for new accounts and updated development rules for AI coding agents.

In a recent development, openRouter is adapting the researchers’ testing approach for ongoing checks and technically verifying network paths to identify requests and responses that may be forwarded to third parties. Removed endpoints will require appropriate assurances and validation before regaining ZDR eligibility.

It has been revealed that novita is verifying the affected processing paths, pursuing deletion of any retained data with MiniMax and improving Partner API labeling and disclosures of relevant providers’ retention policies. For routed inference, the consequence is that ZDR eligibility now rests on validation of the actual request path alongside provider assurances. OpenRouter’s continuing checks leave one central operational question: whether ongoing testing can expose undisclosed forwarding and retention failures before they affect customer data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that at QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, principal security engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a company-wide technical strategy. Drawing on Netflix's experience scaling internal AI agents, the talk argued that a strategy that brings people together can often scale impact further than any code an engineer could write alone.

Behrens explained that the work started when several product strategies, each with its own direction, began to share similar technical risks. Without a common technical strategy underneath them, teams were optimizing locally for different goals. His view was that technical strategy can complement product strategy without waiting for it, that lightweight strategies deliver faster than long technical documents, and that a clear north star does more steering than people expect.

According to recent reports, the talk presented a playbook organized as levels in a video game. The first step is finding the right problem. Behrens suggested looking at company communications, incident trends, technical debt, conversations with other tech leads, and gaps between team charters, then deciding whether the problem is worth solving now, whether it is foundational or compounding, and whether one is the right person to lead it.

It has been revealed that next comes the pitch. Behrens recommended a short problem statement that explains the intent, the expected value, the problems with supporting evidence, why the work matters now, and dated next steps. He suggested leaving possible approaches open so the people who join can shape them, and testing the statement early with a few colleagues, including the likeliest dissenter.

Industry observers note that the presentation then covered building a small tiger team focused on creating the strategy rather than executing it. Behrens highlighted the importance of mixing perspectives, choosing people comfortable with ambiguity, getting manager support, and agreeing on scope, timeline, and a clear stop condition from the start. He shared that his first meeting had far too many people and still missed key functions, and emphasized that the most crucial trait of a good team is making it safe to push back.

According to recent reports, with a team in place, the next step is a north star, a short aspirational statement that gives direction and helps answer whether a piece of work moves the organization closer or farther from its goal. Behrens noted that writing a good north star is harder than it looks, and recommended drafting it with the team and pairing it with key outcomes that define what must be true.

Recent findings suggest that the strategy itself, according to Behrens, is simply a set of choices. He described writing strategy bets as a choice versus another reasonable choice, naming the tradeoff explicitly, keeping each bet short, and revisiting them over time. If a bet does not feel a little uncomfortable, he said, it is probably not a real bet. Keeping only a small set of active bets helps the strategy stay focused.

The talk also emphasized communication and feedback. Behrens suggested expanding support gradually from the immediate team to managers, directors, and executives, recruiting champions across the organization, and openly showing how feedback changed the strategy. Success, he said, is when you are not in the room and people can still explain the work. He also reviewed common failure modes, such as unclear problem statements, the wrong team, vague north stars, bets that are not really bets, and strategies that nobody knows exist.

The presentation concluded by encouraging engineers to keep strategy simple, communicate it widely, use a short north star to steer decisions, and adapt the playbook to their own context. As organizations launch more initiatives in parallel, especially around AI, the ability of senior engineers to align many teams around a shared technical direction may become as valuable as the systems they build.
